documents.abstract: Objective To develop and validate a fully automatic artificial intelligence (AI)-driven system for children with an adenoid hypertrophy (AH) screening based on lateral cephalograms (LCs). Methods A total of 679 LCs obtained from 12-year-old children, including 582 Chinese and 97 Caucasian children, were randomly assigned to a training set (n = 459) to train AI models, a validation set (n = 100) to determine optimal parameter values and a test set (n = 120) to evaluate the AI model’s performance. A five-fold cross-validation was employed to evaluate accuracy. A category-based relation consistency mean teacher network (CRC-MT) model was trained to automatically screen AH. Accuracy, recall, precision and F1 score were used to evaluate the performance of the AI model for AH screening. The AH screening performances of the AI-driven models and manual processing were compared. The accuracies of AI-driven and manual AH detection with blocked regions were also analysed and compared. Results The accuracy and recall of AH screening in full LCs were 80.5%–85.6% and 69.5%–79.5%, respectively; the precision and F1 scores were 67.7%–75.7% and 66.0%–85.9%, respectively. The chi-square test revealed that the AI-driven model achieved higher accuracy in terms of the accuracy, recall, precision and F1 score of AH screening compared with human results. The accuracy of AH screening in the blocked adenoid, airway and jaw was 0.820, 0.883 and 0.892, respectively. The performance of manual AH screening was significantly low in the blocked adenoid, upper airway and jaw region images. Conclusions A fully automatic AI-driven system was developed and validated for the screening of AH in children based on LCs.

Abstract There has been recent interest in smart human–building interaction (HBI) interfaces to improve how occupants interact with building systems. Intelligent facility management (FM) utilizes HBI principles to transform static infrastructures into dynamic, human-centric environments, where facility managers need to interpret live Internet-of-things (IoT) sensor data, consult procedures, and execute safe control actions for various building systems. These tasks are fragmented across dashboards, manuals, and control panels, increasing cognitive load and slowing down decision-making. To address these challenges, this study proposes the multiagent extended-reality and sensing-aware task-level reasoning orchestrator (MAESTRO). MAESTRO is a multimodal agentic GenAI assistant comprised of four agents that support procedural queries, telemetry interpretation, and supervised device actuation in a single HBI loop. MAESTRO integrates a large action model (LAM)-based system with retrieval-augmented reasoning interfaced in an extended reality (XR) environment and mediated by a Model Context Protocol. It uses an orchestrator, which is the coordination component that interprets each user request and decides which agent capability should handle the request, while enforcing supervised and schema validated execution for sensing and actuation. The orchestrator routes each request to the appropriate agents including a domain-adapted FM language agent trained on manuals, logs, and work orders; an IoT control agent that generates schema validated tool calls to sensors and actuators; and a vision language agent for image-based queries. MAESTRO was evaluated on various HBI testing scenarios covering safety inspection, system control, troubleshooting, and procedural guidance. The results show improved language modeling and answer quality after adaptation, a valid tool-call rate of 91%, device-execution success of 89%, telemetry match rate of 81%, and an overall end-to-end task success rate exceeding 84%. This paper shows the potential of integrating fine-tuned LAM-based agents with structured IoT-enabled middleware and XR-based HBI systems, demonstrating how foundation-model reasoning and actuation can support more intelligent and adaptive HBI workflows.

Abstract: This paper draws attention to the urgent need of building Cognitive Infrastructure along with the physical infrastructure for rapid development of the country. India is rapidly transitioning from developing economy to a developed economy unleashing many forces of rapid development and growth. The quest for Vikasit Bharat @2047 (India as a developed country) requires building the foundational cognitive-intellectual infrastructure and not just physical infrastructure. The development of the human capital with higher cognitive abilities capable to create, add and transact value through knowledge creation and utilisation. Continual innovation is critical for sustainable growth and development. Innovation is a direct outcome of the quality of the cognitive infrastructure. Nations compete on the strength of their cognitive infrastructure and not just on the availability of natural resources. Cognitive infrastructure is the most critical factor of production. To build a high-quality competitive cognitive infrastructure we need new ways of acquiring and utilising knowledge. Without cognitive abilities people cannot become knowledge workers to lead the cognitive shift happening all over the world in this age of Artificial Intelligence (AI). The race is now cognitive in nature and those nations with robust cognitive and physical infrastructure will be the leaders. India has to focus on developing the cognitive capital of the aspiring youth equipping the with cognitive abilities to respond to what is coming. The uncertainties caused by technological disruptions and geopolitical shifts are overwhelming. True security comes from building an ever-expanding and renewed cognitive infrastructure which is free from the laws of diminishing returns. This paper explores the need to take a fresh perspective of the emerging realities such as the shift from computing to cognitive, and recommends building futuristic cognitive infrastructure along with the physical infrastructure for realising the goal of Vikasit Bharat @2047. One core concern highlighted is the linguistic development as human development is fundamentally the cultivation of cognitive capacity—and language is one of the most powerful instruments for that cultivation.

Management commitment is the organisational mechanism through which occupational health and safety policies become credible workplace protections, yet evidence from Uganda’s lower-level health facilities remains limited. This study examined the relationship between healthcare workers’ perceptions of management commitment and occupational health and safety policy and their multidimensional well-being in government Health Centre II and Health Centre III facilities in Bushenyi District, Uganda. A cross-sectional convergent mixed-methods design was used. Quantitative data were obtained from 98 of 103 sampled healthcare workers (95.1%), while qualitative data were obtained from 21 of 24 purposively selected healthcare administrators (87.5%). A five-point Likert questionnaire measured management commitment and policy as well as physical, psychological, occupational, and social well-being. Quantitative data were analysed using frequencies, percentages, means, standard deviations, Pearson correlation, and a separate simple linear regression. Interview data were analysed thematically and integrated with the statistical results. All six indicators of management commitment and policy were rated poorly; confidential counselling (M = 1.98, SD = 0.94) and penalty-free mental-health breaks (M = 1.85, SD = 0.88) were especially weak. Perceived management commitment and OHS policy had a strong positive relationship with well-being (r = .748, p < .001) and explained 56.0% of its variance when considered alone (R² = .560, F(1, 96) = 121.94, p < .001). Administrators reported that formal counselling was absent, peer discussion substituted for professional help, and workers feared being labelled weak when disclosing distress. The findings show that written rules are insufficient unless leaders visibly enforce OHS, allocate resources and provide confidential psychosocial support. District and facility managers should establish funded OHS plans, confidential referral pathways, non-stigmatising help-seeking arrangements and documented follow-up to reported concerns.

This study examines voter behavior in the context of the 2024 United States Presidential Election by analyzing user comments from Reddit. Owing to the platform’s anonymity and community diversity, Reddit provides signals that reflect a wide range of socio-demographic perspectives on the electoral process. A dataset of 7,788 comments was collected through the Reddit API and the PRAW library, then preprocessed (cleaning, normalization, stopword removal, and labeling) for sentiment analysis. In the experimental stage, five transformer-based models (BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa, ALBERT, and GPT-2) were comparatively evaluated. Results show that DeBERTa achieved the highest accuracy and F1 scores, while GPT-2 performed relatively poorly in classification tasks. Statistical analyses revealed that 51.6% of Trump-related comments were positive, whereas comments on Harris displayed a more fragmented distribution. Neutral sentiments dominated the “Unknown” category. These findings indicate that Reddit sentiment signals reflect not only descriptive observations but also statistically robust evidence for electoral forecasting. Beyond methodological contributions, the study integrates emotional indicators into the rational-actor assumptions of public choice theory, demonstrating that voter behavior is shaped by both rational and emotional factors. In doing so, it provides an interdisciplinary framework that validates the applicability of artificial intelligence methods to political behavior analysis.

This literature review article establishes cutting-edge methodological strategies for implementing reasonable accommodations in Paraguayan higher education. Under Ludwig Wittgenstein's premise —“the limits of my language mean the limits of my world”— the impact of the educational gap reported by PISA 2025 is analyzed, where 77% of students fail to reach the minimum level in reading comprehension. Confronting the "canned mind", sterile technicism, and post-truth that impoverish academic debate, an imperative return to primary sources (printed or digital) is proposed as a critical and empowering dialogue. Recovering Don Carlos Antonio López's historical mandate to establish classrooms as "monuments to freedom," and combining Ramón I. Cardozo’s New School with Augusto Cury’s neurodidactics, several operational tools are developed: a UDL Andragogical Rubric for comparative law evaluation, a Comprehensive Neurodidactic Intervention Plan focused on bidirectional inclusion and systemic well-being, a Dogmatic Analysis of Teacher Shielding, a Cross-Border Bilingualism Approach, and a proposal for Advanced Curation Training for Learning and Research Resource Centers (CRAI). Furthermore, the use of Generative Artificial Intelligence is declared and methodologized as an advanced aid for citation tracking, data curation, and indexed source recovery.

This research compares three strategies for creating USs: manual, supported by a general-purpose LLM, and supported by a specialized AI Agent. We analyze students' perceptions of the USs produced and the advantages and disadvantages of each approach.

documents.abstract: AlphaEvolve, introduced in A. Novikov et al . [“AlphaEvolve: A coding agent for scientific and algorithmic discovery” (Tech. Rep., Google DeepMind, 2025).], is a generic evolutionary coding agent that combines large language models (LLMs) with automated evaluation in a loop that proposes, tests, and refines algorithmic solutions. Here we showcase AlphaEvolve as a tool for autonomously discovering novel mathematical constructions and making progress on long-standing open problems. On 67 problems spanning mathematical analysis, combinatorics, geometry, and number theory, the system rediscovered the best known solutions in most cases and improved on them in several. In some instances, it also generalized results for finitely many input values into a formula valid for all inputs. Furthermore, we combine this methodology with Deep Think [Google DeepMind, Advanced Version of Gemini with Deep Think Officially Achieves Gold-Medal Standard at the International Mathematical Olympiad (Google DeepMind Blog, 2025).] and AlphaProof [Google DeepMind, AI Achieves Silver-Medal Standard Solving International Mathematical Olympiad Problems (Google DeepMind Blog, 2024).] in a broader framework where the additional proof assistants and reasoning systems provide automated proof generation and further mathematical insights. These results demonstrate that LLM-guided evolutionary search can autonomously discover mathematical constructions that complement human intuition, at times matching or improving the best known results, and point to new modes of interaction between mathematicians and AI systems. AlphaEvolve explores vast search spaces to solve complex optimization problems at scale, often with significantly reduced preparation and computation time.

Background/Objectives: The mechanical performance of spinal instrumentation depends on appropriate fixation of rod-securing screws. Although manufacturer-recommended torque values and torque-limiting instruments are widely used in spinal surgery, the contribution of surgeon-related factors to manually applied tightening torque remains insufficiently characterized. This study aimed to quantify the magnitude and variability of tightening torque applied by spine surgeons and to investigate the influence of handling technique and surgeon orientation on torque generation. Methods: A thoracolumbar spine model instrumented with pedicle screw–rod constructs was used in an experimental setup. Twenty-two spine surgeons from six institutions performed a total of 220 screw-tightening procedures using a standardized manual screwdriver setup. Tightening torque was estimated from measured loosening torque using a previously established calibration relationship. Hand usage, hand position, and surgeon orientation relative to the construct were recorded. Statistical analyses were performed to compare torque values between different handling conditions. Results: The mean estimated tightening torque was 4.52 Nm, with considerable inter-individual variability among surgeons. Two-handed grip produced significantly (p = 0.006) higher torque (5.76 ± 1.46 Nm) compared to thumb-downward (3.47 ± 1.19 Nm). Among the univariate linear regression analyses, only the two-handed grip technique showed a significant association with higher fastening torque (B [95% CI]: 1.88 [0.56; 3.21], p = 0.008). The other factors (age, height, weight, experience) did not show a significant relationship. Conclusions: Manual tightening torque during spinal instrumentation shows substantial variability among surgeons and is influenced by handling technique and surgeon position. These findings demonstrate the importance of considering human factors in biomechanical evaluations of spinal fixation procedures. Further studies are required to determine the clinical significance of this variability.

Agents built on large language models (LLMs) now browse, fill in forms and complete transactions on websites that were designed for people looking at a screen. Existing standards do not describe what such an agent needs from a page. WCAG 2.2 sets requirements for human users of assistive technology, and interoperability standards assume two systems that already share a structured contract. Neither says when a web interface can be reliably perceived, acted on and recovered from by an autonomous agent. This paper proposes the Agent Accessibility Measurement Framework (AAMF) to fill that gap. AAMF divides the construct into Core In-Page Accessibility, made up of Structural Interpretability (SI), Semantic Richness (SR), Action Executability (AE) and Resilience and Error Recoverability (RR), and a separate Machine Discoverability and Protocol Support (MDP) pillar. We define 25 indicators with explicit formulas, an equal-weight baseline score, a failure-criticality-weighted composite score, and a five-layer Agent Interaction Stack (AIS) that keeps in-page interaction apart from out-of-band discovery. We place the construct within ISO/IEC 25010:2023, work through one hypothetical scoring example, and derive 25 engineering guidelines from the indicator definitions. The paper specifies the framework only. It reports no audit of production websites and no agent task study; Section VII describes the study that is needed to validate it.

Train drivers are exposed to prolonged sitting and whole-body vibration (WBV) during train operation, which may increase the risk of musculoskeletal disorders. This study assesses the WBV exposure levels and estimated the prevalence of neck pain and low back pain (LBP) among train drivers. WBV exposure was evaluated for six train drivers using A (8) and vibration dose value (VDV (8)) in accordance with ISO 2631-1:1997 and EU Directive 2002/44/EC. A crosssectional survey involving 51 train drivers was conducted using socio-demographic and occupational questionnaires, as well as the Standardised Nordic Questionnaire, the Neck Disability Index (NDI), and the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI). The mean A (8) and VDV (8) values (1.174 m/s² and 35.0 m/s1.75, respectively) exceeded the Exposure Action Value and Exposure Limit Value. A high prevalence of LBP (78.4%), as well as upper and lower neck pain (49.0% and 47.1%, respectively) was observed. Respondents reported functional limitations related to neck pain, while 64.7% of drivers had moderate to severe disability associated with prolonged sitting and ergonomic strain. These indings highlight the need for effective control measures to reduce WBV exposure and mitigate the impact on musculoskeletal health among train drivers.

PURPOSE: Medical leadership is essential for high-value care, yet organisational conditions remain variable. This study aims to examine whether clinicians' motivation and perceived readiness to lead are matched by enabling infrastructures (e.g. protected time, decision support and shared-governance routines) and how gaps relate to perceived impact and clinician wellbeing. DESIGN/METHODOLOGY/APPROACH: The authors conducted an anonymous, cross-sectional online survey distributed internationally via professional networks and snowball sampling. Descriptive analyses compared clinicians and non-clinician leaders on five-point Likert items. Exploratory models assessed associations between cumulative "support deficits", perceived leadership impact and stress/burnout. In addition, a Shared-Governance Alignment Index was constructed. The survey was open from 4 November 2025 to 17 December 2025 and eligible respondents were clinicians or non-clinician healthcare leaders able to report on leadership, organisational support or clinician-administrator collaboration within their healthcare setting. FINDINGS: A total of 143 responses were analysed (107 clinicians; 36 non-clinician leaders), predominantly from Italy (76%). Clinicians reported strong interest in leadership roles [median 5 (4-5); 88% agree/strongly agree] and high self-rated preparedness [median 4 (4-5); 80% agree/strongly agree], but limited organisational supports, particularly protected time for leadership/quality improvement [median 2 (1-3)] and constrained access to decision support tools [median 3 (2-4)]. Increasing cumulative support deficits showed a dose-response relationship with lower perceived leadership impact (e.g. endorsement that leadership improves care quality: 94% with 0 deficits versus 53% with 2 deficits) and higher odds of stress/burnout. Clinicians also rated shared-governance conditions less favourably than non-clinician leaders, indicating persistent perceptual misalignment in clinician-administrator collaboration. RESEARCH LIMITATIONS/IMPLICATIONS: This study used a voluntary, cross-sectional survey, limiting causal inference and increasing susceptibility to self-selection, common method and social desirability biases. Measures relied on self-report rather than objective indicators of governance quality, decision-support availability or performance outcomes. The international, network-based sampling may under-represent some regions, specialties and non-clinician perspectives. Nonetheless, findings generate testable propositions for longitudinal and mixed-methods research examining how protected time, shared-governance routines and decision-support infrastructure influence leadership effectiveness and clinician wellbeing and whether closing the motivation-support gap improves organisational outcomes. Future studies should incorporate administrative data. PRACTICAL IMPLICATIONS: Organisations should complement leadership development with structural protections: defended time, accessible decision-support tools and clear shared-governance routines (co-owned decisions and aligned metrics). Without these supports, clinician motivation may translate into strain rather than sustained improvement. SOCIAL IMPLICATIONS: Strengthening medical leadership through protected time, decision-support and shared governance can yield broader social benefits beyond organisational performance. When clinicians and administrators co-own improvement priorities, care processes become more reliable, reducing avoidable harm and enhancing public trust in health services. Better-supported leaders may also curb burnout and turnover, stabilising the workforce that communities depend on. More inclusive governance structures can amplify frontline and patient voices, supporting equity in service redesign and ensuring scarce resources are allocated transparently and ethically. These conditions may improve access, particularly for marginalised groups during pressures. ORIGINALITY/VALUE: The study frames medical leadership as an organisational capability and identifies a "motivation-support gap". By associating self-reported structural deficits with perceived effectiveness and wellbeing, it offers actionable targets to strengthen clinician-administrator partnership and leadership sustainability. The revised framing also explicitly situates medical leadership within digital readiness, artificial intelligence-enabled decision support and health-information-system adoption as contemporary components of organisational support.

The purpose of this article is to present more fundamentally the natural metabolism of science and the scientific journal, partly using examples from radiology. The journal article is the main tool and practice of the researcher in converting personal knowledge into public knowledge for its verification and pragmatic realization. In national medicine and radiology, there is a problem of long-term preservation of knowledge (the work of scientists and state finances) and its accessibility against the backdrop of the emergence of new journals and their disappearance. If earlier there was a problem with the publication of articles due to the shortage of journals and the queue for publication, now there is a problem with the shortage of high-quality content articles. Virtually all significant results in the exact sciences (at least in the English-speaking world) can be found in the pages of just two journals: “Nature” and “Science”. Lotka’s law is mentioned in the aspect of the scientific literature citation system as a means of tracking the development of science. Attention is drawn to the formation of a new subspecialty – medical writers (since 1940). The replication crisis is described (possibly caused by human factors), a methodological crisis in which the results of many scientific studies are difficult or impossible to reproduce. The mobilization of science in the journal “Radiation diagnostics, radiation therapy” during the COVID-19 pandemic is considered using the example of articles “Low-dose radiation therapy for COVID-19 pneumonia”, “COVID-modulated emphysematous pyelonephritis against the background of severe course of oxygen-dependent covid pneumonia” та “Echocardiographic characteristics of complicated course of coronavirus infection in children (COVID-19) (review and portfolio)”. The bibliometrics of the journal “Radiology” (journal of the Radiological Society of North America.) are presented for comparison: the most viewed articles of 2021 and the most cited articles of 2021. It is demonstrated that the topic of the most cited articles of 2023 is artificial intelligence.

Microphysiological systems (MPS) have emerged as transformative in vitro platforms to address the long-standing bottlenecks of conventional preclinical models, including poor physiological relevance inherent to 2D cultures, as well as species incompatibility and ethical constraints associated with animal models, thereby improving clinical predictability and redefining modern pharmaceutical development. This review highlights the innovative convergence of bioprinting, organoids, organ-on-a-chip (OoC), and artificial intelligence (AI) as a next-generation MPS framework, enabling precision reconstruction of human tissue microenvironments with unprecedented fidelity. Bioprinting delivers spatially defined 3D architectures; organoids recapitulate organ-specific heterogeneity; OoC integrates dynamic physiological cues; and AI enables intelligent fabrication optimization, real-time monitoring, and predictive drug-response modeling. Their synergistic integration overcomes the inherent limitations of single-technology systems. We emphasize state-of-the-art MPS applications in disease-drug screening, and toxicological assessment across tissues and multiorgan crosstalk models, underscoring their paradigm-shifting potential. Remaining challenges, such as long-term functional maturation, vascularization complexity, and standardized validation, and future directions, including multi-cue integration, modular scalability, and AI-driven in vitro-in vivo correlation, are concisely outlined. This interdisciplinary synthesis establishes MPS as a cornerstone technology to accelerate pharmaceutical innovation, reduce reliance on animal models, and advance precision medicine toward clinical translation, thereby filling a critical gap in current biomedical research.

Mineralogical composition and crystal structure govern not only the geological classification of ore-derived dust but also its biological reactivity, yet the mineralogy–toxicity relationship of respirable dust from metal and nonmetal (MNM) mining operations remains poorly constrained. This study presents a mineralogical and physicochemical characterization of laboratory-generated respirable dust from bulk ore collected at one metal mine and four nonmetal mines, spanning five geological settings. Mineral phase and crystal structure were identified by XRD, with FTIR, SEM-EDX, and ICP-MS providing complementary structural, morphological, and elemental data. Crystalline silica (quartz) dominated four of five mine dust types (70.0%–88.3% in silica-rich nonmetal samples; 78.5%–86.6% in the metal mine), confirming pervasive respirable crystalline silica exposure regardless of commodity, while one nonmetal mine yielded a silica-free, carbonate-dominated dust as a reference material. In vitro MTT assays showed dose-dependent cytotoxicity across all samples, with viability at 100 µg/mL ranging from 31% to 71%. Quartz-rich nonmetal dust reduced viability to ~45% versus ~62% for carbonate-dominated dust (p ≤ 0.0001), while metal mine dust was most cytotoxic (31%–44%), coinciding with elevated surface manganese. This potency gradient (carbonate < silica-rich nonmetal < metal) establishes direct, mineralogically grounded structure–toxicity relationships and provides foundational data for occupational health risk assessment and dust control in MNM mining environments.

documents.abstract: Previous studies of artificial intelligence (AI)-driven automation have mostly assessed entire occupations, providing limited evidence about differences among individual tasks. This study addresses this limitation by proposing an NLP-assisted task-level assessment framework for estimating the automation potential of journalistic work. Of the 30 task descriptions listed for the O*NET occupation “News Analysts, Reporters, and Journalists” (27-3023.00), 25 were retained following scope-based screening and grouped into ten composite tasks representing the focal news-production workflow. Each task was assessed across three dimensions—Verb Type, Social Dependence, and Skill Type—using NLP-assisted feature extraction and structured consensus-based evaluation. The resulting component scores were combined into a composite automation potential score ranging from 0 to 1. Editing visual content and filing stories obtained the highest estimated scores (0.97), followed by gathering background information and collecting media content (0.77). Arranging interviews (0.20), conducting interviews (0.23), and receiving assignments to develop story ideas (0.27) received the lowest estimated scores. The study contributes a transparent and interpretable proof-of-concept approach for operationalizing task-level automation potential across procedural, social, and skill-related dimensions. The resulting scores represent relative task-level estimates rather than observed rates or probabilities of workplace automation. With larger labeled task datasets, the three dimensions defined in this framework could provide a basis for supervised classification and subsequent predictive modeling of automation potential across broader task collections.

documents.abstract: The production of granulated compound feed in livestock enterprises is a complex technological process that requires precise monitoring of physical and chemical parameters. Ensuring efficiency and quality in this process demands advanced modelling and management approaches. The study aims to develop a methodology for modelling compound feed production through information-analytical systems and to define the principles of process management. The research is based on a systematic review of literature studies. After applying relevance and thematic selection criteria, 16 sources were retained for the final review and included in the reference list. The methodology combines literature review, comparative analysis, and synthesis. The analysis shows that effective modelling of feed production requires hybrid applications of deterministic, statistical, neural network, and fuzzy logic approaches. Information-analytical systems must adopt a multi-level architecture covering field operations, process monitoring, production management, and business planning. Artificial intelligence technologies – particularly machine learning, deep learning, and reinforcement learning – demonstrate high efficiency in quality prediction, anomaly detection, and the development of optimal management strategies. According to the comparative synthesis of the reviewed literature, the application of information-analytical systems can reduce raw material loss by 28–35%, decrease product quality variation by 58–62%, optimize energy consumption by 18–24%, increase production productivity by 20–30%, reduce deviation from plan by 67–75%, shorten technical downtime duration by 30–40%, and decrease quality control labour expenditure by 57–60%.Conclusion. For Azerbaijan, it is recommended to design systems that account for regional raw material bases, climatic conditions, and the technical capacity of local enterprises. The study confirms that the digital transformation of the feed industry is a multifaceted challenge requiring coordinated efforts among academic institutions, industrial enterprises, and governmental bodies.

Science literacy is an important aspect of science learning, yet students continue to face challenges in developing this competency. This condition is reflected in the initial science literacy test results of seventh-grade students at SMPN 1 Klangenan, Cirebon Regency, which showed an average score of 59.1, with a mastery rate of only 28.5%, below the minimum mastery criterion of 70. One effort to address this issue is to develop teaching materials that integrate problem-based learning with engaging and contextual visual media. This study aimed to develop and examine the validity, practicality, and effectiveness of a Problem Based Learning (PBL) science module integrated with an educational comic on the rain cycle theme to improve the science literacy of seventh-grade students. The study employed a mixed-methods approach using the ADDIE (Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, Evaluation) development model. The educational comic was developed with the assistance of artificial intelligence technology and Canva. The results showed that the developed module was highly valid, with an average validity score of 90.5%, and highly practical, with 91.3% positive student responses. The module was also effective in improving science literacy, as indicated by an N-Gain of 0.64 in the experimental class, higher than 0.36 in the control class. The difference in science literacy improvement was statistically significant based on the Mann-Whitney U test (p = 0.002), with a large effect size (Cohen’s d = 0.94). The highest improvement occurred in the indicator of identifying scientific issues, with an N-Gain of 0.69. Thus, the AI-assisted, comic-integrated PBL module is a valid, practical, and effective science teaching material for improving junior high school students’ science literacy. ABSTRAK Kemampuan literasi sains peserta didik merupakan salah satu aspek penting dalam pembelajaran IPA, tetapi masih menghadapi berbagai tantangan. Kondisi tersebut tercermin dari hasil tes awal literasi sains peserta didik kelas VII SMPN 1 Klangenan, Kabupaten Cirebon, yang menunjukkan rata-rata nilai 59,1 dengan ketuntasan belajar sebesar 28,5%, masih di bawah KKM 70. Salah satu upaya untuk mengatasi permasalahan tersebut adalah mengembangkan bahan ajar yang mampu mengintegrasikan pembelajaran berbasis masalah dengan media visual yang menarik dan kontekstual. Penelitian ini bertujuan mengembangkan, menguji kevalidan, kepraktisan, dan keefektifan modul pembelajaran IPA berbasis Problem Based Learning (PBL) yang diintegrasikan dengan komik edukatif bertema siklus hujan untuk meningkatkan literasi sains peserta didik kelas VII. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan mixed methods dengan model pengembangan ADDIE (Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, Evaluation). Komik edukatif dikembangkan dengan bantuan teknologi kecerdasan buatan dan Canva. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa modul yang dikembangkan sangat valid dengan rata-rata kevalidan 90,5% dan sangat praktis dengan respons positif peserta didik sebesar 91,3%. Modul juga terbukti efektif meningkatkan literasi sains, ditunjukkan oleh N-Gain kelas eksperimen sebesar 0,64, lebih tinggi dibandingkan kelas kontrol sebesar 0,36. Perbedaan peningkatan literasi sains kedua kelas signifikan berdasarkan uji Mann-Whitney U (p = 0,002) dengan effect size besar (Cohen’s d = 0,94). Peningkatan tertinggi terjadi pada indikator mengidentifikasi isu ilmiah dengan N-Gain sebesar 0,69. Dengan demikian, modul PBL terintegrasi komik berbasis AI merupakan bahan ajar IPA yang valid, praktis, dan efektif untuk meningkatkan literasi sains peserta didik SMP.

The smartphone alarm app is one of the most used applications in the world, yet HCI research has paid relatively little attention to how people actually use it beyond the canonical wake-up. The smartphone has substantially extended the alarm’s reach – making it a portable instrument for shaping attention, structuring tasks, and disciplining a future self. Drawing on a survey of 70 participants and 15 in-depth interviews, this paper documents how participants used alarms as a tool to support intention offloading, artfully adopting its simple structure to initiate, structure and end future activity. Participants talked about alarms as a way of disciplining their future self – an attempt to force oneself to attend to some task, even if the later self might be resistant. In our discussion, we develop two readings of this practice: alarms as cognitive offloading and alarms as a ‘technology of the self’, and we use the tension between these to mount a critique of the meta-cognitive framework that has dominated recent treatments of reminder use. We close by exploring how alarms could be re-designed to maintain their power as a ‘tough friend’ while supporting new collaborative and less-stressful practices.

documents.abstract: Ambient sensors offer a privacy-preserving solution for activity recognition in smart homes, yet they face a critical challenge in multi-resident environments known as Data Association, which aims to identify the resident triggering a specific anonymous sensor event. Existing approaches fundamentally fail to maintain global consistency by often yielding conflicting associations for silent residents. Additionally, these methods frequently suffer from severe trajectory fragmentation caused by the ontological mismatch of applying continuous physical motion models to discrete logical behaviors. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework that reformulates data association as a sequential decision-making task within a Markov Decision Process (MDP). We solve the defined MDP via Behavior Cloning (BC) to avoid complex reward engineering by directly learning from expert demonstrations. We instantiate the policy using two complementary architectures, including a lightweight Transformer that treats association as a multi-label classification task over linearized event histories, and a fine-tuned Large Language Model (LLM) that reformulates the problem as conditional text generation to leverage pre-trained semantic knowledge. Extensive evaluations on three diverse datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, particularly in resolving concurrent multi-resident events. Furthermore, the LLM-based policy shows preliminary cross-environment transfer potential under benchmark settings, while its robustness in real deployments still requires further validation.

Self-talk is a meaningful psychological signal that reflects individuals' emotions, motivations, and cognitive states, yet remains difficult to capture in daily life. It often emerges spontaneously during moments of pressure, concentration, or repeated decision-making, making it a relevant target for behavioral and cognitive interventions such as Educational Self-Talk Intervention (ESTI). However, ESTI largely depends on expert observation or retrospective self-reports, which are limited in capturing fleeting self-talk patterns and hinder its scalability in real-world settings. To address this gap, we present MutterMeter, a mobile self-talk detection system that continuously analyzes audio from earable microphones and classifies utterances into Negative self-talk, Positive self-talk, and Others. Focusing on tennis as a high-pressure and cognitively demanding testbed, MutterMeter employs a hierarchical framework that integrates acoustic, linguistic, and contextual information while adaptively balancing accuracy and efficiency. Evaluated on a first-of-its-kind dataset we collected (34.5h, n=29), MutterMeter achieves a macro-averaged F 1 score of 0.815 across subjects, outperforming baselines such as LLM-based models and speech emotion recognition models. Moreover, its adaptive processing pipeline reduces unnecessary computation by finalizing confident cases early, while maintaining robust detection performance.

Generative artificial intelligence increasingly mediates university students' access to Islamic knowledge, posing challenges for scholarly legitimacy, evidentiary accuracy, and accountability. This article offers a conceptual framework for negotiating religious authority and verification at universities in Banten, Indonesia. Integrative literature review incorporates scholarly perspectives on Islamic authority, digital religion, algorithmic authority, source credibility, epistemic vigilance, AI literacy, and Islamic educational ethics. Purposefully selected academic writings, policy documents, and institutional data are compared and synthesized with the use of thematic analysis. Synthesis reveals the distinction between acknowledged religious legitimacy and epistemic authority which is achievable through accessibility and fluency without interpretive competency and accountability of scholars. Verification process consists of seven steps involving classification of questions, identification of claims, authentication of evidence, independent comparison, contextual interpretation, consultation, and decision-making closure. This article proposes a multi-dimensional negotiation of religious epistemic authority as a conceptual framework that allows assigning different roles to algorithms, texts, ulama, lecturers, and institutions. Four heuristic orientations exemplify potential scenarios of reliance and verification. Banten is used as the background, but not the empirical field site, of the analysis. Both the conceptual framework and the heuristic orientations have not been tested yet. Contribution of the study is the religiously-grounded approach to verification which will prove useful for the development of Islamic religious education, assessment, university governance, and will allow proposing research directions for future comparative analysis.

The vision of Viksit Bharat @2047 represents India's aspiration to emerge as a developed, inclusive, innovative, technologically advanced and knowledge-driven nation by the centenary of its independence. The achievement of this vision depends substantially on the quality of human capital developed through education. School education, in particular, has a foundational role because the students educated today will become the professionals, entrepreneurs, researchers, teachers, administrators, innovators and responsible citizens who will shape India's social and economic development in the coming decades. In this context, the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, digital transformation and skill-based education have emerged as three interconnected dimensions of educational reform. NEP 2020 seeks to transform Indian education through a holistic, multidisciplinary, flexible and competency-oriented approach. It emphasizes foundational literacy and numeracy, experiential learning, critical thinking, creativity, vocational education, multilingualism, technology integration and the development of 21st-century competencies. The policy also recognizes that digital technologies can support teaching-learning, assessment, teacher development and access to educational resources. At the same time, the rapid development of artificial intelligence, digital platforms, virtual learning environments, educational applications and data-driven systems is changing the nature of teaching and learning. Digital transformation, however, should not be understood merely as the replacement of textbooks with screens or classrooms with online platforms. It requires a fundamental reconsideration of pedagogy, curriculum, assessment, teacher competencies and learner participation. Skill-based education is equally important for preparing learners for a changing world of work. Traditional education that primarily emphasizes the accumulation and reproduction of information may not adequately prepare students for employment, entrepreneurship, innovation and lifelong learning. Future-ready learners require a combination of academic knowledge, digital literacy, communication, collaboration, creativity, critical thinking, problem-solving, financial awareness, entrepreneurial thinking, vocational competencies and social-emotional skills. The present paper critically examines the relationship between NEP 2020, digital transformation and skill-based education in the context of Viksit Bharat @2047. The study adopts a qualitative conceptual and analytical research design based on secondary sources, including policy documents, government publications, international reports and relevant academic literature. The analysis identifies four major dimensions of transformation: policy reform, technological transformation, competency development and educational equity. The study argues that technology can significantly enhance educational opportunities, but its effectiveness depends upon teacher preparedness, appropriate pedagogy, infrastructure, accessibility, digital safety and meaningful integration into the curriculum. UNESCO similarly emphasizes that technology should support education rather than replace human interaction and that equitable access, appropriate governance and teacher capacity are essential conditions for effective digital transformation.

documents.abstract: Next-Generation Cybersecurity: Architectural Resilience, Threat Paradigms, and the Shift to Zero-Trust in Distributed Ecosystems 1. Introduction: The Disappearing Walls of the Digital World For decades, cybersecurity operated on a simple mental model: the Castle-and-Moat. An organization built massive stone walls (firewalls) and dug deep moats around its physical office. Anyone outside was considered an enemy, and anyone inside was trusted by default. Once an employee crossed the drawbridge with an ID badge or a VPN password, they had broad access to wander the corridors of the castle—opening file cabinets, browsing internal servers, and viewing databases. This model worked well when every worker sat at a desk in the same building, using a desktop computer plugged into a company wall socket, accessing a server located in the basement. Today, that castle has dissolved: Distributed Ecosystems: Applications no longer run on single servers in the basement. They live spread across global cloud providers (Amazon, Google, Microsoft), edge devices, and remote home offices. Ephemeral Workloads: Many modern services run inside "containers"—tiny virtual programs that spin up in seconds to handle traffic and vanish minutes later. Hybrid Work: Employees access critical databases from home Wi-Fi networks, hotel lounges, and mobile phones across multiple time zones. Because there is no longer a physical perimeter to defend, treating the "inside" of a network as safe has become one of the most dangerous assumptions in computing. Next-generation cybersecurity replaces this outdated perimeter with two foundational principles: Zero-Trust Architecture (ZTA) and Architectural Resilience. 2. Modern Threat Paradigms: How Attackers Actually Operate To understand why security models had to change, we must look at how modern cyberattacks work. Attackers rarely smash directly through the front gates anymore; they use subtle, compound techniques designed to exploit implicit trust. A. Lateral Movement (The Hotel Keycard Problem) In an old network, once an attacker cracked a single, low-priority device—like a smart thermostat or an intern’s laptop—they were "inside." From there, they could quietly move sideways across the network (lateral movement), hopping from computer to computer until they found high-value assets like customer databases or payroll systems. It is the equivalent of a hotel where your room keycard can open every other bedroom door, the manager's office, and the bank vault downstairs. B. Supply-Chain Poisoning Modern software is rarely written entirely from scratch. Developers build applications by assembling hundreds of pre-existing open-source building blocks (libraries and packages). Attackers now target these third-party ingredients rather than the company itself. By quietly injecting malicious code into an upstream component that thousands of companies rely on, attackers gain an automatic backdoor into hundreds of corporate environments simultaneously. C. Identity as the New Attack Surface Attackers do not "hack" their way in using cinematic decryption tools; they simply log in using stolen credentials. Through phishing, credential stuffing, or purchasing stolen session tokens on the dark web, adversaries pose as legitimate users. If a network grants broad trust based purely on a correct password, the attacker inherits that trust instantly. 3. The Core Shift: Demystifying Zero-Trust The core philosophy of Zero-Trust is simple: Never trust, always verify. In a Zero-Trust architecture, the concept of a "trusted internal network" does not exist. Every request—whether coming from an unknown laptop in an airport cafe or an executive workstation inside headquarters—must prove its identity, validate its device health, and prove its authorization for every single interaction. Think of it like moving from a castle drawbridge to an international airport security model: Having an airline ticket does not let you wander onto the tarmac. You show your passport at the security line. You show your boarding pass at the gate. You are checked again as you step onto the aircraft. You are only permitted to sit in your designated seat, not enter the cockpit. How a Zero-Trust Policy Engine Evaluates a Request Every time an entity (a person or an automated software service) asks to read or write data, an automated "Policy Engine" inspects four distinct layers before granting access: Evaluation Factor What the System Checks Everyday Analogy Who is asking? Cryptographic identity, multi-factor authentication (MFA). Showing a government passport with a matching biometric scan. What device are they using? Device posture (operating system patched? disk encrypted? antivirus running?). Ensuring the vehicle entering a military base has passed safety inspections. Where are they located? Contextual clues (unusual time of day, anomalous geographic location, impossible travel speed). Flagging a credit card charge in Tokyo two hours after a purchase in London. What do they need? Least-privilege authorization (only the exact file or micro-service needed right now). A hotel keycard programmed to unlock only Room 304, and only until checkout. The Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP) Under Zero-Trust, access is no longer a blanket pass. It is granular and temporary. If an accountant needs to review a single invoice, they receive access only to that specific document for the duration of the task. They do not get read-access to the entire financial repository. 4. Architectural Resilience: Assuming the Breach Traditional security aimed for 100% prevention, an impossible standard in systems with millions of lines of code. Next-generation cybersecurity embraces an engineering reality known as Assume Breach. Resilience means accepting that software will have bugs, passwords will leak, and human users will occasionally click malicious links. The objective of the architecture is to guarantee that when a component fails or is compromised, the entire system does not collapse. A. Microsegmentation (Watertight Bulkheads) In maritime engineering, modern ships like ocean liners are divided into compartmentalized bulkheads. If a rock tears a hole in the outer hull, water fills only that single chamber. The water-tight doors slam shut, preventing the ocean from flooding the rest of the ship. In cybersecurity, this is called microsegmentation. Instead of a vast, flat corporate network where every device can talk to every other device, the digital ecosystem is divided into hundreds of isolated micro-zones: The web server can talk to the application server. The application server can talk to the database. The web server can never communicate directly with the database. Individual employee laptops cannot communicate with one another at all. If an attacker compromises one device, their "blast radius" is zeroed out. They are trapped inside that single isolated room. B. Security Chaos Engineering How do engineers know their defenses will hold during an attack? They deliberately simulate attacks during regular operations. Borrowed from Netflix's concept of the "Chaos Monkey," modern security teams use automated tools that deliberately shut down servers, revoke authentication certificates, or simulate rogue network traffic in real-time. By continuously exposing systems to artificial failures, the infrastructure develops an "immune system," learning to self-heal, reroute traffic, and isolate anomalies before a real adversary strikes. 5. The Evolution: Comparing Security Generations To see the complete picture, we can trace how cybersecurity has evolved across three major eras: Dimension Generation 1: Perimeter Defense Generation 2: Defense-in-Depth Generation 3: Zero-Trust & Resilience Primary Mindset Keep the bad actors out. Add layers (antivirus, email filters, firewalls). Assume breach; continuously verify everything. Network Structure Flat internal network; open communication inside. Segmented networks (VLANs, DMZ zones). Microsegmented; every service isolated by default. Trust Model Binary (Trusted inside / Untrusted outside). Role-based, long-lived access tokens. Context-driven, dynamic, least-privilege tokens. Defense Strategy Castle walls and static gatekeepers. Multiple checkpoints with delayed alerts. Automated immune response; self-healing workloads. 6. Emerging Frontiers: AI and the Post-Quantum Horizon As distributed ecosystems mature, two emerging forces are accelerating the need for architectural resilience: Artificial Intelligence at the Edge: Attackers now use machine-learning models to craft bespoke phishing emails in real-time and discover obscure configuration errors automatically. In response, modern defense systems rely on behavioral AI engines that spot anomalous activity in milliseconds—such as an internal account downloading files ten times faster than its daily average—and immediately sever its connection without waiting for human intervention. Post-Quantum Cryptography: The mathematical encryption algorithms safeguarding today's internet (such as RSA and ECC) will eventually be vulnerable to sufficiently powerful quantum computers. Resilient architecture requires "crypto-agility"—the capacity to swap out underlying encryption standards across distributed microservices via software updates, without needing to rewrite entire operating platforms. 7. Conclusion Next-generation cybersecurity is not a single product, firewall, or piece of software you can purchase and install. It is a fundamental philosophical and architectural shift. Cryptographic identity, multi-factor authentication (MFA). Showing a government passport with a matching biometric scan. What device are they using? Device posture (operating system patched? disk encrypted? antivirus running?). Ensuring the vehicle entering a military base has passed safety inspections. Where are they located? Contextual clues (unusual time of day, anomalous geographic location, impossible travel speed). Flagging a credit card charge in Tokyo two hours after a purchase in London. What do they need? Least-privilege authorization (only the exact file or micro-service needed right now). A hotel keycard programmed to unlock only Room 304, and only until checkout. The Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP) Under Zero-Trust, access is no longer a blanket pass. It is granular and temporary. If an accountant needs to review a single invoice, they receive access only to that specific document for the duration of the task. They do not get read-access to the entire financial repository. 4. Architectural Resilience: Assuming the Breach Traditional security aimed for 100% prevention, an impossible standard in systems with millions of lines of code. Next-generation cybersecurity embraces an engineering reality known as Assume Breach. Resilience means accepting that software will have bugs, passwords will leak, and human users will occasionally click malicious links. The objective of the architecture is to guarantee that when a component fails or is compromised, the entire system does not collapse. A. Microsegmentation (Watertight Bulkheads) In maritime engineering, modern ships like ocean liners are divided into compartmentalized bulkheads. If a rock tears a hole in the outer hull, water fills only that single chamber. The water-tight doors slam shut, preventing the ocean from flooding the rest of the ship. In cybersecurity, this is called microsegmentation. Instead of a vast, flat corporate network where every device can talk to every other device, the digital ecosystem is divided into hundreds of isolated micro-zones: The web server can talk to the application server. The application server can talk to the database. The web server can never communicate directly with the database. Individual employee laptops cannot communicate with one another at all. If an attacker compromises one device, their "blast radius" is zeroed out. They are trapped inside that single isolated room. B. Security Chaos Engineering How do engineers know their defenses will hold during an attack? They deliberately simulate attacks during regular operations. Borrowed from Netflix's concept of the "Chaos Monkey," modern security teams use automated tools that deliberately shut down servers, revoke authentication certificates, or simulate rogue network traffic in real-time. By continuously exposing systems to artificial failures, the infrastructure develops an "immune system," learning to self-heal, reroute traffic, and isolate anomalies before a real adversary strikes. 5. The Evolution: Comparing Security Generations To see the complete picture, we can trace how cybersecurity has evolved across three major eras: Dimension Generation 1: Perimeter Defense Generation 2: Defense-in-Depth Generation 3: Zero-Trust & Resilience Primary Mindset Keep the bad actors out. Add layers (antivirus, email filters, firewalls). Assume breach; continuously verify everything. Network Structure Flat internal network; open communication inside. Segmented networks (VLANs, DMZ zones). Microsegmented; every service isolated by default. Trust Model Binary (Trusted inside / Untrusted outside). Role-based, long-lived access tokens. Context-driven, dynamic, least-privilege tokens. Defense Strategy Castle walls and static gatekeepers. Multiple checkpoints with delayed alerts. Automated immune response; self-healing workloads. 6. In response, modern defense systems rely on behavioral AI engines that spot anomalous activity in milliseconds—such as an internal account downloading files ten times faster than its daily average—and immediately sever its connection without waiting for human intervention. Post-Quantum Cryptography: The mathematical encryption algorithms safeguarding today's internet (such as RSA and ECC) will eventually be vulnerable to sufficiently powerful quantum computers. Resilient architecture requires "crypto-agility"—the capacity to swap out underlying encryption standards across distributed microservices via software updates, without needing to rewrite entire operating platforms. 7. Conclusion Next-generation cybersecurity is not a single product, firewall, or piece of software you can purchase and install. It is a fundamental philosophical and architectural shift. The NOVA Q / EIT Genius Model is a conceptual and operational research framework for classifying genius structures — new, valuable, non-trivial informational structures that establish a recognizable structural identity and become fertile sources of further valid structure. The direct object of classification is the structure, not a person or AI system; system-level capability is treated as an indirect inference requiring repeated, held-out, cross-task evidence. The framework defines a five-gate operational core (G1 Novelty, G2 Value, G3 Non-Triviality, G4 Structural Identity, G5 Fecundity), evaluated relative to a frozen reference frame C_ref(field, T0). It prohibits any universal numerical "genius score" and uses a gate matrix with fail-closed statuses (PASS / FAIL / PENDING / NOT_TESTABLE / UNRESOLVED). Its primary application domain is AI and human–AI systems. It specifies validation rules including cipher (reversible-encoding) controls, round-trip tests, target-medium validity, held-out consequences, negative and boundary controls, per-evaluator recognition audits against LLM hindsight leakage, graded fecundity with independence confidence (F0–F4), and role separation between framework constructor, target system, evaluator and auditor. The framework builds on established creativity research (including Boden; Runco & Jaeger; Csikszentmihalyi; Amabile; Simonton; Newell & Simon) and records these relationships in a reference and lineage audit (28 references). It deliberately diverges from systems models of creativity by treating value (G2) as domain validity rather than social acceptance. Status: test-ready conceptual model, frozen with notes (see audit receipt and freeze record). All five gates remain PENDING when applied to the framework itself. It is not an established psychological or neuroscientific definition of genius, and it makes no physical, AGI or ASI claims. Este depósito reúne cuatro archivos con dos versiones del ensayo de José M. Rivera García en español y sus traducciones al inglés: la versión extensa, con referencias, y la versión breve «Primero piensa tú; después pregúntale a la IA», preparada para prensa y revistas. Ambas tratan sobre crianza, aprendizaje, pensamiento crítico y soberanía cognitiva en el uso de la inteligencia artificial. This deposit contains four files: the extended Spanish essay, including references, and the shorter version, “Think for yourself first; then ask AI,” prepared for press and magazines, along with English translations of both. The essays discuss parenting, learning, critical thinking, and cognitive sovereignty in the use of artificial intelligence.

Vision-Language Models (VLMs) transfer visual and textual data into a shared embedding space. In doing so, they enable a wide range of multimodal tasks, while also raising critical questions about the nature of machine ›understanding‹. In this paper, we examine how Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods can render the visual reasoning of a VLM – namely, CLIP – legible in art-historical contexts. To this end, we evaluate seven methods, combining zero-shot localization experiments with human interpretability studies. Our results indicate that, while these methods capture some aspects of human interpretation, their effectiveness hinges on the conceptual stability and representational availability of the examined categories.

How do we promote human capacity for caring and evolving carefully together as we face ecological shifts in habitat and social relations? Using de la Cadena and Blaser’s idea of uncommon(ing) and Judith Butler’s challenge to the common, this paper considers conceptual forms of enclosure and foreclosure that stifle responses to uncertainty. It argues that ideas and identities are being foreclosed by the semantic connections and grammars of digital interaction and AI, much as commons enclose land. Regarding the physical and virtual as parallel spaces of appropriation under capitalist-colonialist cultures, the paper suggests that, if we are to care well, the data processing that feeds computation and artificial intelligence needs reconsideration at its core, much as land use does. If machine “learning” were based on a performative model, rather than something fundamentally categorical, it might avoid the obvious foreclosures of applying static models to changing contexts. Using this analysis, the paper explores data, land, access and inclusion to consider climate care and a transition from infrastructures to world-changing. In the process, the paper examines the linguistic infrastructures that inhibit change.

The EU Artificial Intelligence Act obliges providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems to generate, keep and hand over records: automatically generated logs, technical documentation, and information supplied to authorities on request. A market of "AI governance tooling" is forming to produce those records. This paper asks a narrow question that the Act does not answer: who can check such a record, and with what? If the only software able to read and verify an evidence record is sold by the party whose customer produced it, then regulators, notified bodies and affected persons depend on that vendor's goodwill, pricing and survival. We call this the verification asymmetry. We first set out, cautiously and from the primary texts, how EU law treats open source today: the AI Act's exclusions and carve-outs (Article 2(12), Article 25(4) as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, Article 53(2), recitals 89 and 102-104); the Cyber Resilience Act's definition of free and open-source software and its "open-source software steward" regime (Articles 3(14), 3(48), 24, 25 and 64(10)); and the one place we found where Union law requires open-source licensing of trust-critical software, the European Digital Identity Wallet (Article 5a(3) of Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 as amended). We then examine four precedents in which open verification became shared infrastructure - Certificate Transparency, ACME and Let's Encrypt, Sigstore, and reproducible builds - and identify what made them work, including the parts that have nothing to do with licensing. We compare three places a vendor could draw the line - everything open; open verification with commercial operation; closed with escrow and authority access - and their consequences for regulators, deployers, affected persons and vendors. We argue that the verification side (format specifications, verifier implementations, test vectors) has the economic character of infrastructure and should be open, while value-added operation can remain commercial, and we make recommendations to policymakers and standardisation bodies. The paper is conceptual: it reports no measurements and takes no position on any particular company's licensing decisions.

documents.abstract: Human activity is a fundamental component of intelligent interactive systems. Existing human activity recognition (HAR) follows a closed-ended assumption—defining a fixed set of activity classes and classifying each sensor signal into one of them—yet real-world human behavior is complex and ever-changing and thus cannot be fully represented by any fixed set. We present a new paradigm for open-ended human activity understanding (HAU), shifting the goal from closed-set classification to understanding activities via their meta-motions. To achieve this, we design MOSAIC, a motion decomposition and semantic fusion framework that transforms raw sensor streams into structured meta-motion representations and subsequently generates fine-grained natural-language descriptions. Additionally, we propose an LLM-driven training strategy for sensor-language alignment, enabling effective cross-modal supervision in the absence of real-world training data. Finally, we leverage LLM-assisted reasoning to recognize complex high-level activities based on the understanding of underlying motions and their composition. Our model demonstrates strong generalization and performance across 18 public HAR datasets, outperforming the best baseline by up to 19.6% in unseen scenarios.

In response to persistent limitations in college English instruction in non-English-speaking contexts, this study develops an integrated pedagogical framework combining Task-Based Language Teaching (TBLT), the ARCS motivational model (Attention, Relevance, Confidence, and Satisfaction), Moodle-supported learning activities, and selected intelligent-computing tools for instructional analysis. A Chinese vocational university is used as the instructional context. The framework is designed to connect authentic or quasi-authentic language tasks with motivational scaffolding, structured online resources, learner feedback, and data-informed evaluation. The study examines learner engagement, perceived comprehensibility, English-skill performance, motivation-related indicators, score dispersion, and a structural model of the proposed teaching framework. The results presented in the source materials indicate higher levels of reported participation and classroom attention in the ARCS-supported condition than in the comparison condition. Skill-level comparisons also show gains in several reading- and discourse-oriented indicators, while some listening and speaking outcomes remain comparatively resistant to improvement. The structural model suggests that attention, confidence, satisfaction, intrinsic motivation, and perceived relevance are interrelated, although the reported relevance-to-motivation path is not statistically significant (p=0.218). The findings are interpreted descriptively because the supplied material does not provide a complete participant register, raw dataset, validated measurement protocol, or full inferential-statistical specification. The study therefore supports the pedagogical value of integrating task design, motivational support, and digital learning resources while calling for more rigorous future evaluation of AI-assisted adaptive learning and data-driven instructional optimization.

Medical specialist training in South Africa is undergoing a significant transformation, as training programmes adopt work-based learning, workplace-integrated learning and workplace-based assessment (WBA) as part of their pedagogy. This is in keeping with a global move towards evidence-based educational processes. Workplace-based assessment emerged from competency-based medical education (CBME), but instead of using simulation for teaching and assessment, it is integrated into real-world clinical practice. This enhances the validity of teaching, learning and assessment, given the inherent focus on safe and effective patient care. It is context-rich and, given that most of the global literature emanates from high-income countries, a publication that speaks directly to contextual factors in low-middle-income contexts became necessary. This book is an output of ongoing collaboration between a group of South African medical educationists, managers and clinician leaders, who started working together in 2022. It presents a synthesised approach to implementing WBA in resource-constrained contexts and takes into account the unique cultural, social and relational nature of clinical teaching and learning that cannot be ignored when considering such a significant system transformation. We do this by framing the work within an Ubuntu-inspired pedagogy. The book remains true to the technical aspects of a WBA programme, with each chapter dealing with a specific component of WBA. The reader is taken from an introduction to the key concepts, the social dynamics of the supervisor–trainee dyad, the inner workings of workplace learning, teaching and assessment, to the summative process of the clinical competency committee (CCC). Chapter 7 deals with the requirements of a digital information system, and the final chapter details the change management process that we followed, highlighting some lessons and achievements. The addenda are composed of a series of brief ‘how-to’ documents that could inform the development of standard operating procedures.

BackgroundHuman-AI collaboration is increasingly shaping platform-based work, yet workers may struggle to develop a sense of ownership over work produced under algorithmic management. Psychological ownership may provide an important mechanism for understanding sustainable human-AI work.ObjectiveThis study examines how human-AI value alignment and task complementarity influence psychological ownership and worker outcomes, and whether algorithmic transparency conditions these relationships.MethodsTwo empirical studies were conducted with platform-based gig workers, comprising 217 participants in Study 1 and 209 in Study 2. Study 1 examined psychological ownership as a mediator of the relationships between human-AI design features, eudaimonic well-being, and occupational resilience. Study 2 examined algorithmic transparency as a moderator and tested moderated mediation using bootstrapped PROCESS analyses.ResultsHuman-AI value alignment and task complementarity positively predicted psychological ownership, which, in turn, was associated with greater eudaimonic well-being and occupational resilience. Psychological ownership significantly mediated these relationships. Algorithmic transparency strengthened the effects of both design features on ownership and their indirect effects on well-being and resilience.ConclusionsPsychological ownership is a central mechanism through which human-AI job design contributes to sustainable work. Algorithmic transparency functions as an enabling condition that allows workers to verify alignment, contribution, and agency.

documents.abstract: This article theoretically and practically analyzes the pedagogical and psychological opportunities for developing independent thinking in students within a digital information environment. It is substantiated that the widespread penetration of digital technologies, internet resources, e-learning platforms, and artificial intelligence tools into the higher education process not only expands students' opportunities for working with information but also creates risks such as ready-made information perception, cognitive dependence, superficial acquisition, and a decrease in independent thinking activity.

This community service activity aims to address the low digital literacy competence and the technical difficulties faced by early childhood educators in producing interactive learning media, particularly at TK 'Aisyiyah Bustanul Athfal Koya Timur, Jayapura. Grounded in the challenges of conventional video editing software and administrative burdens, the program implemented a Participatory Action Research (PAR) method structured into problem identification, planning, implementation, and evaluation phases. The training involved 19 participants, consisting of kindergarten teachers, lecturers, and university students, focusing on the practical integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT and Google Flow. The results demonstrate that participants successfully mastered digital ethics, visual criteria for early childhood based on IDAI standards, and precision prompting techniques using the "ASIH" formula. Furthermore, teachers successfully produced independent, child-friendly animated video learning media. The technical barriers, such as network instability and platform quotas, were effectively resolved through mobile hotspots and alternative account management. In conclusion, this Artificial Intelligence training significantly enhances teachers' practical digital skills and provides an innovative, sustainable solution to strengthen early childhood literacy in the digital age, while reinforcing that technology serves as a support tool alongside the primary role of educators' mindful presence and empathy.

PT Tiran Indonesia merupakan pertambangan nikel yang menggunakan dump truck sebagai transportasi utama dalam pengiriman barang tambang dari lokasi penambangan ke tempat penyimpanan atau pelabuhan untuk pengiriman lebih lanjut. Berdasarkan data dari PT Tiran Indonesia masih terdapat angka kecelakaan yang cukup signifikan terkait pengoperasian dump truck di perusahaan tersebut. Penyebab utama dari kecelakaan ini adalah faktor manusia sebanyak 67% dan tindakan tidak aman sebanyak 64%. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mengetahui tingkat situation awareness pengemudi dump truck di PT Tiran Indonesia dalam melakukan pekerjaannya dengan metode Quantitative Analysis of Situational Awareness (QUASA). Hasil penelitian diketahui nilai actual situation awareness sebesar 66% dan nilai perceived situation awareness sebesar 79% serta nilai situation awareness sebesar 50% disimpulkan bahwa tingkat situation awareness pengemudi dump truck berada pada kategori rendah. Hal ini menunjukkan bahwa pengemudi dump truck belum sepenuhnya waspada dalam bekendara karena masih melakukan tindakan yang tidak sesuai dengan standar operasional prosedur yang berlaku.

This study examined students’ perception on challenges associated with using artificial intelligence (Chat GPT) in learning science in senior secondary schools in Kaduna North Local Government Area, Nigeria. The research design was a cross-sectional survey research design. The population of the study consisted of eight co-educational schools having a total number of two thousand nine hundred and forty three (2,943) of SS III students across the eight secondary schools in Kaduna North Local Government Area. From the population of the study 352 students were selected to form the sample size for the study. The instrument used for data collection was a structured Students ‘Artificial Intelligence Opinion Questionnaire (SAIOQ). The reliability coefficient of the instrument was 0.81. The study was guided by two research questions and two null hypotheses tested at the 0.05 level of significance. Descriptive statistics of frequencies and percentages were used to answer research questions, Chi-square (ꭓ2) statistics was used to test null hypotheses. The result of the finding showed no significant difference between students’ perceptions and the challenges associated with the use of Chat GPT among secondary school students in Kaduna North. Based on these findings, it was therefore recommended that, students should be trained on the responsible use of Chat GPT. Schools should organize orientation programmes, seminars, and workshops to teach students how to use Chat GPT as a supplementary learning tool while avoiding overdependence on AI-generated responses.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI)-generated feedback is increasingly transforming mathematics education by providing timely, personalized, and adaptive learning support. However, limited evidence exists on the behavioural mechanisms through which students’ perceptions of AI-generated feedback influence mathematics learning outcomes, particularly in Sub-Saharan Africa. This study examined the direct and indirect relationships among Perceived AI Feedback Quality (PAQ), AI Dependence (AID), and Mathematics Learning Outcomes (MLO) among 360 undergraduate students in Ghana. A quantitative cross-sectional survey design was adopted, and data were analysed using Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) with IBM SPSS Statistics 23 and AMOS 23. The measurement model demonstrated satisfactory reliability and validity. The structural model showed that PAQ significantly predicted AID ( β = 0.673, p < .001) and MLO ( β = 0.449, p < .001), while AID also significantly predicted MLO ( β = 0.441, p < .001). Bootstrapping analysis further revealed that AID partially mediated the relationship between PAQ and MLO ( β = 0.314, p < .001). The findings indicate that students who perceive AI-generated feedback as accurate, relevant, and useful are more likely to depend on AI, and this dependence is in turn associated with stronger perceived mathematics learning outcomes. The study extends Feedback Theory and Social Cognitive Theory by identifying AI Dependence as a key behavioural mechanism linking AI feedback quality to mathematics learning. The findings provide practical implications for educators, instructional designers, and policymakers seeking to promote the effective and responsible integration of AI technologies into mathematics education.
