documents.abstract: Abstract Electricity demand from data centers is rising quickly with the deployment of artificial intelligence (AI), and cooling remains the largest non-IT load, particularly in hot-arid climates. This paper presents a performance analysis of leveraging AI to reduce the energy consumption of a 10 MW AI/cloud data center located in Abu Dhabi. A component-level energy model is developed that couples server and accelerator power, uninterruptible power supply (UPS) losses, airflow and hot-air recirculation, server-fan penalties, air-cooled chiller efficiency and dry-cooler economization. On this digital twin, a five-layer framework integrates a long short-term memory (LSTM) load forecaster, a double deep Q-network (DDQN) that sets supply-air temperature, chilled-water temperature and airflow under a digital-twin safety shield, forecast-driven server consolidation and thermal-aware shifting of flexible workloads. Trained on one synthetic year and tested on an independent year against a static baseline, an ASHRAE-optimized rule-based strategy and model-based oracle bounds, the LSTM gives the lowest day-ahead error (MAPE 3.04%). The complete framework reduces annual facility energy by 15.3% (13.85 GWh), cooling energy by 40.8% and peak demand by 14.1%, and improves power usage effectiveness (PUE) from 1.421 to 1.291, while holding the 99th-percentile rack inlet temperature below 27°C. It captures 99.9% of the oracle-attainable saving and pays back in 1.7 years under stated assumptions. The results also show that PUE alone can misrepresent AI-driven savings.

This study aims to describe the perceptions of Primary School Teacher Education (PGSD) students at Universitas Riau, cohort 2025, regarding the use of ChatGPT as a support tool for mathematics learning. The study employed a quantitative approach with a descriptive design. The sample consisted of 50 students selected using purposive sampling based on the criteria that they had used ChatGPT to support mathematics learning or mathematics assignments. Data were collected through an online questionnaire using a five-point Likert scale consisting of 30 initial statements. The instrument was tested using Pearson item-total correlation for validity and Cronbach’s Alpha for reliability. The results showed that 18 statements were valid, with a Cronbach’s Alpha value of 0.926. The analysis showed that perception scores ranged from 52 to 90, with a mean of 67.40 and a standard deviation of 8.54. A total of 33 students (66%) were categorized as having high perceptions, 12 students (24%) as moderate, and 5 students (10%) as very high. No respondents were categorized as low or very low. These findings indicate that students who have used ChatGPT tend to have positive perceptions of its use as a support tool for mathematics learning. ChatGPT can support mathematics learning activities while students remain responsible for verifying information and understanding the solution process.

documents.abstract: Background Noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL) remains an important occupational health problem, especially in high-intensity noise work settings. Although disposable foam earplugs (DFE) are widely used, the protection they provide depends on how well they are fitted. We examined initial earplug attenuation in military aviation personnel, the change observed after individualized on-site instruction and repeat fitting among participants initially below target, and the association between previous instruction and baseline attenuation. Methods This retrospective, single-center observational study analyzed routinely collected occupational-health fit-testing data from 183 military aviation personnel evaluated between 2020 and 2022. Mean age was 22.84 ± 6.23 years, and 91.3% were male. Earplug attenuation was measured using the 3M E-A-Rfit Dual-Ear Validation System. Participants with mean binaural attenuation below 20 dB received individualized on-site instruction and repeated the fitting procedure. Results During initial fitting, 118 participants (64.5%) did not achieve the 20 dB target. In this group, mean binaural attenuation rose from 14.47 to 22.57 dB after instruction and repeat fitting, an improvement of 8.10 dB ( p < 0.001). Participants who reported having received previous earplug-use instruction also had higher baseline attenuation than those without previous instruction (19.47 vs. 16.52 dB; p = 0.002). Conclusion Quantitative fit testing identified inadequate initial attenuation in nearly two-thirds of the personnel assessed. Brief individualized instruction followed by repeat fitting was associated with a substantial improvement in attenuation among those initially below target. Incorporating personal fit testing and targeted instruction into occupational hearing-conservation programs may improve protection against NIHL.

Our goal is to offer proof of concept for the idea that behavioral networks emerging with and beyond assigned treatment networks in experiments can provide a valuable window on agency. We call these often unobserved behavioral structures phantom networks. Most evidence of agency is entangled with audience — what people recall, how others attribute, or who is seen to act. We strip that away to observe agency directly in the ties participants build within and beyond what they are assigned. Their deviation from assignment is not error but structure-in-action, a behavioral trace of agency. We offer three exhibits of that “behavioral deviation” revealing agency in gendered brokerage, rival brokerage, and structural reproduction. Across the three exhibits, behavioral deviation shows how a team works (sometimes in surprising ways), not how well the team works. Teams perform as expected in theory, but the behavior responsible for their performance is made more apparent by watching behavioral deviation. We close with a summary proof of concept and discussion of next steps for particularly promising future work

When new therapeutic interventions are developed, clinical trials become an essential part of the drug development process to establish efficacy and safety. However, these trials also expose patient to unknown risks and adverse reaction which can addressed with help of pharmacovigilance. The World Health Organization defines pharmacovigilance as the science of detecting, assessing, understanding, and preventing adverse drug reactions or other drug-related problems. It plays a critical role in ensuring patient safety during clinical trials. Effective pharmacovigilance involves systematic monitoring and reporting of adverse events, maintaining data integrity, and continuously evaluating the benefit–risk balance of investigational products. By integrating ethical principles, Good Clinical Practice (GCP) guidelines, and modern technologies such as electronic data capture, artificial intelligence, and real-world evidence, pharmacovigilance enhances the reliability of clinical research and safeguards patient welfare. This review article highlights the processes, challenges, and future directions of pharmacovigilance in clinical trials, emphasizing its importance in the development of safe and effective medicines.

The pharmaceutical management information system (SIMF) has the potential to improve the efficiency of prescription services, but the relationship with perceived service quality is influenced by infrastructure readiness, integration, and users. Evidence from Puskesmas that links the level of SIMF implementation with efficiency and quality is still limited. To analyze the relationship between SIMF implementation and the efficiency and quality of prescription services perceived at the Palembang City Health Center and explain the obstacles to implementation. Sequential mixed-methods explanatory research was conducted in six health centers in 2026. Cross-sectional surveys of 18 pharmacists (total sampling) and 96 patients were followed by semi-structured interviews with 6 pharmacists to explain the survey findings. The analysis included descriptive statistics, Shapiro–Wilk tests, Spearman correlation (with simple linear regression as sensitivity analysis), and exploratory MANOVA; interviews were analyzed thematically. High implementation was found in availability and use (94.4%), usefulness (94.4%), and convenience (88.9%), while resources and infrastructure were mainly in the moderate category (77.8%). Wait times ≤20 minutes were experienced by 90.6% of patients and 87.5% were very satisfied. Implementation was positively associated with efficiency (rs=0.512; p=0.030), but not significantly associated with perceived quality (rs=0.404; p=0.097); inconclusive due to limited testing power). Interviews showed that data flow and prescribing readability improved, but unstable connections, limited computers, double record-keeping, absence of clinical decision support, and uneven training still occurred. Higher implementation of SIMF was associated with better operational efficiency, but was not significantly associated with perceived quality (inconclusive due to limited testing power); interviews indicated that quality may be limited by sociotechnical gaps and integration. Strengthening infrastructure, interoperability, clinical decision support, and ongoing training are needed.

This paper specifies the Planetary Health Axis System (PHAS), An active learning framework integrating data, large language models, and human experts for planetary health. The system is a pipeline of eight stages: (1) leakage-free preprocessing, mixture-of-experts imputation, and credibility-weighted data integration; (2) extraction of a dynamic, context-dependent knowledge prior from the scientific literature by a domain-tuned large language model; (3) nIDE non-invertible, asymmetric dimensionality expansion with median-kernel aggregation; (4) SCGL conditional structural graph learning on the lifted representation under a generalized-sparse, locally-dense, hub-mediated structure with acyclicity; (5) an active-learning, human-in-the-loop closure that converts learned structure into staged, verifiable queries; (6) non-discounted long-run-average optimal control subject to generalized planetary-boundary constraints, yielding KKT shadow prices and propagated top-level weights; (7) numerical solution by relative-value or policy iteration, with evaluation of the current state against the constrained optimum; and (8) full-system path/flux attribution together with unconditional and conditional distributional extrapolation. Together, the eight stages form a coupled estimation-and-control procedure that converts heterogeneous planetary-health evidence into verifiable structure and, ultimately, into boundary-respecting, decision-facing policies.

User-generated content (UGC) is increasingly used to inform heritage planning, yet platform visibility may not reflect the spatial elements that require management attention. Using Hangzhou Steel Park as a case study, this study compares 3521 online posts (containing 18,827 images in total) from four platforms with 2689 protocol-based on-site images. A multimodal large language model converted images into structured descriptions, which were analysed with BERTopic. Three linked models compared online and on-site visual topics, tested robustness through downsampling, and examined post-level image–text integration. Online UGC concentrated on blast furnaces, night lighting, check-ins, and visitor experience, whereas the on-site reference provided broader coverage of renovated buildings, vegetation, lawns, corridors, and other spatial elements. The leading blast-furnace topic remained dominant after downsampling, suggesting that corpus size alone is unlikely to explain its prominence. Post-level discourse analysis remained strongly experience-oriented. These findings show that UGC is valuable for monitoring visitor attention but should be complemented by systematic on-site evidence for spatial planning and heritage management.

Abstract Artificial intelligence and smart technologies are rapidly evolving, opening up new opportunities for economic progress, but also raising complex ethical questions. Technological paradigms concentrate on efficiency, optimization, and material progress, but often lack the inherent frameworks to deal with existential, moral, and socio-cultural consequences. In this paper, it is argued that literature is an indispensable moral compass for ethical integration of AI, more so in the setting of national growth and sustainable development (like India’s Viksit Bharat vision). This study draws on contemporary post-human literature, eco-critical texts, and speculative narratives to argue that literary humanities provide algorithmic development critical empathy, ethical foresight, and socio-cultural grounding. This paper employs a qualitative, interdisciplinary methodology drawing on Post-Humanist Theory, Narrative Ethics and Hermeneutics to explore how literary tropes challenge technological determinism and articulate human-centric technological futures. The results show that it is impossible to achieve long-term national development based only on scientific innovation, and that a synergistic relationship between technical ability and humanistic ethics is necessary. This paper thus presents practical recommendations for the incorporation of literary studies into STEM curricula, AI ethics policy, and multidisciplinary research frameworks, to ensure that national technological progress is ethically grounded, socially inclusive, and humanely sustainable.

Detailed postural assessment is crucial in the construction sector due to the high physical demands, awkward positions, and repetitive manual tasks that contribute to work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WRMSDs). This study aimed to evaluate ergonomic risk levels and their association with musculoskeletal discomfort among Malaysian construction workers using an integrated approach combining the Rapid Entire Body Assessment (REBA) and the Ovako Working Posture Analysis System (OWAS). Integrating both tools provides a comprehensive assessment as REBA captures task-specific biomechanical loads, while OWAS reflects cumulative postural stress during static and dynamic tasks. A cross-sectional study was conducted at four construction sites involving 106 workers. Musculoskeletal discomfort was assessed using the Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire (NMQ), capturing symptoms over the past 12 months and 7 days. Postural risks were quantified using two complementary ergonomic tools the Rapid Entire Body Assessment (REBA) and the Ovako Working Posture Analysis System (OWAS)through video analysis and structured field observations. Within the past 7 days, the most reported musculoskeletal symptoms were localized to the lower back (64.2%), wrists/hands (50.8%) and shoulders (49.1%). REBA analysis revealed that 73.6% of workers were exposed to high to very high ergonomic risk, with fibre installers exhibiting the highest mean score (11.2 ± 2.1). OWAS evaluation indicated that 58.4% of observed postures fell into Action Categories 3 or 4, signifying a need for prompt corrective intervention A strong positive correlation between REBA and OWAS scores (r = 0.61, p < 0.01) demonstrated consistent identification of postural risks, particularly among ironworkers and carpenters. Chi-square analysis further confirmed significant associations between elevated ergonomic risk levels and reported discomfort in the lower back and shoulders (p < 0.05). The integrated use of REBA and OWAS provides a robust ergonomic evaluation framework that can guide targeted interventions and inform policy to reduce WRMSDs among construction workers.

Within the operating room, the anesthesia work environment (AWE) has been a primary contributor to healthcare associated infections (HAIs). This is usually attributed to a lack of hand hygiene compliance in anesthesia professionals. However, due to the fast-paced and complex nature of the AWE, a complete picture of how infectious agents spread throughout the AWE is unknown. This paper describes a novel computational approach using formal verification with model checking that can prove whether the cleanliness of each item within a model of an AWE is maintained and, if not, show how the failure occurred. We applied this method to the analysis of the anesthesia induction process of the Auckland Academic Health Alliance. We use the results of this analysis to recommend hand hygiene interventions that will address discovered problems.

Generative AI increasingly allows learners to obtain mathematical output without performing all of the cognitive work through which competence is formed. This preprint proposes a theoretical framework for competency-level, process-replacing AI delegation in mathematics education. Mathematical competencies are represented by a prerequisite network. Learner mastery and AI-delegation intensity are modeled separately, while a strictly downstream prerequisite centrality measures how strongly later competencies depend on a given skill. A mastery gate provides local protection against premature delegation independently of graph position. The resulting framework distinguishes three factors: what the learner has already mastered, how much cognitive work is delegated to AI, and how structurally important the competency is for subsequent learning. A continuous optimization model is introduced as an analytical relaxation, together with a discrete classroom interpretation. Monte Carlo stress tests compare graph-aware and simpler delegation policies at equal immediate productivity under several structural data-generating mechanisms. The graph-aware policy is deliberately shown to perform worse when downstream prerequisite structure is irrelevant, and to become advantageous only when downstream propagation is sufficiently important. A 25-competency case study in measure theory, probability, martingales, and mathematical finance illustrates the framework. The paper concludes with a preregistrable empirical hypothesis: the effect of a process-replacing AI-access regime on later autonomous mathematical performance should become less favorable when baseline unmasteredness and downstream prerequisite centrality are jointly high. This is a theoretical and simulation-based preprint. No human-subject experimental results are reported.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: One-handed interaction on large-screen smartphones often leads to ergonomic discomfort and disruption, while existing solutions typically rely on explicit gestures, additional hardware, or static ergonomic models, limiting their deployability and adaptability. We present PreTap, an anticipatory system that implicitly infers reachability and predicts imminent tap regions from zero-permission inertial signals, enabling proactive interface adaptation during the pre-tap phase. Realizing this capability introduces challenges, including the extremely short prediction horizon, substantial inter-user variability in reachability zones, and IMU signal patterns. To address these challenges, PreTap combines an on-device (i.e., 180K-parameter) CNN-Attention model with an unsupervised reachability analysis algorithm that captures user-specific ergonomic constraints and supports user-specific adaptation goals. An empirical study with 50 participants on commodity smartphones shows that PreTap can accurately predict the tap intent and proactively adapt the UI approximately 220 ms before contact, while maintaining low runtime overhead suitable for real-time deployment. These results demonstrate the potential of implicit motion sensing to enable intelligent, reachability-aware mobile interfaces that better align with users' motor intent.
topics: Personal Information Management and User Behavior

documents.abstract: Procedural tasks with multiple ordered steps are ubiquitous in daily life. Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have enabled personal assistants that support daily activities. However, existing systems primarily provide reactive guidance triggered by user queries, or limited proactive assistance for isolated short-term events rather than long-horizon procedural tasks. In this work, we introduce Pro 2 Assist, a step-aware proactive assistant that continuously tracks fine-grained task progress and reasons over the user's evolving state to provide timely assistance throughout tasks. Pro 2 Assist leverages multimodal data from augmented reality (AR) glasses to achieve motion-based perception. It then extracts step-oriented procedural context from multi-scale temporal dynamics and task-specific expert knowledge. Based on both sensory input and procedural context, Pro 2 Assist performs continuous reasoning to infer user needs and display timely assistance on AR glasses. We evaluate Pro 2 Assist using a dataset curated from public sources and a real-world dataset collected on our testbed with AR glasses. Extensive evaluations show that Pro 2 Assist outperforms the best-performing baselines by over 21% in procedural action understanding accuracy, and it achieves up to 2.29X the proactive timing accuracy of baselines. A user study with 20 participants further shows that 90% find Pro 2 Assist useful, indicating its effectiveness for real-world procedural assistance.

Large language models (LLMs) frequently endorse and elaborate on users’ delusional beliefs, a failure mode termed psychogenicity in the Psychosis-Bench study of Au Yeung et al., whose framing we adopt. We present the first systematic evaluation of whether anti-sycophancy interventions transfer to psychosis-relevant contexts. Across 1,280 experiments spanning 10 conditions, 8 frontier LLMs, and 16 clinically derived Psychosis-Bench scenarios, a combined anti-sycophancy prompt reduces mean Delusion Confirmation Scores by 73.8% (paired \(t(127)=11.74\) , \(p<10^{-21}\) , Cohen's \(d=1.04\) ). Adding a domain-general self-reflection prompt yields a 77.0% reduction and raises Safety Intervention rates by 66.9%, delivered entirely as a system prompt. Classifier-based guardrails (Llama Guard 3) flag only 5 of 3,072 evaluated turns; a reasoning guardrail (o4-mini) flags \(14\times\) more. Ablations isolating either mechanism alone plateau at \(\approx 46\%\) reduction, establishing anti-sycophancy prompting as a necessary foundation that add-on mechanisms augment but cannot replace.

documents.abstract: The integration of generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education is transforming curriculum development by enabling AI systems to contribute to the design of learning outcomes, assessments, instructional activities, and other curriculum artefacts. Despite growing interest in AI literacy, prompt engineering, and human–AI collaboration, limited attention has been given to how educators enact curriculum expertise within AI-mediated design environments. This conceptual paper introduces the Prompt-Mediated Curriculum Development (PMCD) framework, which conceptualises curriculum development as an iterative process of human–AI co-design mediated through prompt literacy. Drawing on curriculum theory, sociocultural perspectives on mediation, human–AI collaboration, and AI literacy scholarship, the framework positions prompt literacy as the central mechanism linking educator expertise, agentic AI systems, and curriculum artefacts. Prompt literacy is defined as the ability to formulate, refine, and evaluate prompts in ways that support pedagogically aligned and contextually relevant educational outcomes. Building on the framework, the paper proposes a Prompt Literacy Taxonomy comprising three developmental levels: Foundational Prompting, Pedagogical Prompting, and Agentic Orchestration. The taxonomy provides a conceptual basis for understanding how educators engage in sophisticated forms of AI-supported curriculum development. The paper contributes to the literature by advancing prompt literacy as a distinct form of educational expertise, proposing a theoretical model of AI-mediated curriculum development, and offering a developmental taxonomy to inform future research, faculty development, and institutional AI integration strategies.

Abstract Objectives To compare automated mucus plug detection with radiologist evaluation, assess AI-assisted detection, and examine associations of algorithm-derived airway obstruction burden with COPD severity. Materials and methods This retrospective analysis included 278 COPDGene participants selected across never-smokers, smokers with preserved ratio-impaired spirometry, and GOLD stages 0–4. An AI tool generated candidate plugs. Two thoracic radiologists independently identified plugs in unaided and AI-assisted sessions. A third thoracic radiologist adjudicated all candidates as the reference. Patient- and plug-level performance, observer agreement, false-positive detection, and rank-transformed associations with pulmonary function, CT parameters, and clinical severity were evaluated. Results Reference mucus plugs were present in 114/278 participants (41%). Patient-level AI sensitivity was lower than R1 (68.4% vs 86.8%; p < 0.001) but not different from R2 (68.4% vs 79.8%; p = 0.141), whereas specificity was similar across approaches (95.7% vs 98.8%–100.0%). Plug-level AI sensitivity was lower than both readers (34.8% vs 58.9% for R1 and 55.6% for R2; both p < 0.001). AI assistance improved readers’ plug-level sensitivity (63.6–68.6%; p ≤ 0.004). AI-reader agreement was good (κ, 0.62–0.69), and inter-reader agreement improved with AI (κ, 0.70 vs 0.78; p < 0.001). These non-reference-positive AI detections (0.396/scan) were mostly marked bronchial wall thickening or partially occlusive mucus. They were independently associated with worse airflow limitation, CT emphysema, Pi10, and clinical severity after accounting for true-positive burden, improving model fit (Δ R ², 0.03–0.05). Conclusion AI was less sensitive than radiologists but had similar specificity for mucus plug detection. AI assistance improved reader sensitivity and agreement. Additional algorithm-detected airway abnormalities remained associated with airway disease severity. Key Points Question Automated mucus plug detection on chest CT may enable standardized COPD assessment, but independent validation against radiologist assessments remains limited . Findings Artificial intelligence showed lower sensitivity than radiologists but similar patient-level specificity on chest CT, and assistance improved sensitivity and inter-reader agreement . Clinical relevance Automated mucus plug analysis may support standardized airway obstruction burden assessment in COPD research and clinical trials while retaining radiologist oversight .

Generative artificial intelligence has rapidly reduced the distance between imagining a creative artifact and producing it. Images, videos, written works, advertisements, illustrations, and other forms of media that once required substantial time, labor, technical expertise, or financial resources can now be generated with comparatively little production effort. This paper examines the distinction between whether something can be produced and whether producing it is appropriate, useful, accurate, relevant, or communicatively successful. Using the framework of Red Tape Theory™, the paper investigates the proposition: Just because we can does not mean we should. The proposition is not presented as an argument against artificial intelligence, generative media, or technological experimentation. Rather, it examines the possibility that increased technological capability can create a tendency to treat capability itself as justification for use. The paper develops a series of distinctions: CAPABILITY ≠ APPROPRIATENESSNOVELTY ≠ VALUETECHNICAL QUALITY ≠ COMMUNICATIVE SUCCESSBEAUTY ≠ ACCURACYATTENTION ≠ UNDERSTANDINGPRODUCTION EFFICIENCY ≠ CREATIVE JUSTIFICATIONCAN ≠ SHOULD Three observational contexts are examined. First, the author’s use of generative AI across different creative tasks demonstrates the importance of task-dependent utility and tool selection. OpenAI systems have been used for conceptual development, thesis writing, philosophical exploration, poetry, and children’s literature, while other generative systems have been used for more straightforward visual-production tasks. This comparison is presented not as a universal ranking of AI systems, but as an example of a tool-agnostic, purpose-first approach to creative technology. Second, publicly documented NFL–Adobe implementations of generative AI are examined as an example of AI being incorporated into a large-scale brand and content ecosystem. The case illustrates how generative technology can be used for content scaling, personalization, workflow efficiency, governance, and brand-oriented production while simultaneously raising questions about the relationship between technical possibility and communicative relevance. Third, the paper examines brand appropriateness and the possibility that an artifact may be technically sophisticated while remaining poorly aligned with the identity, purpose, audience, or context for which it was created. The paper proposes that creative evaluation should distinguish at least five dimensions: Capability — Can the system produce the requested artifact?Accuracy — Does the artifact correctly represent its subject?Quality — Is the artifact technically and aesthetically successful?Relevance — Does it serve the communication objective?Appropriateness — Does it belong within the brand and audience context? These dimensions should not be collapsed into a single judgment of whether an artifact is simply “good.” Within Red Tape Theory™, the resulting decision process is: PURPOSE → AUDIENCE → IDEA → TOOL → OUTPUT → OBSERVATION → QUESTION → ADJUSTMENT rather than: CAPABILITY → FIND SOMETHING TO USE IT FOR The paper further examines the consequences of reduced production friction. When generative systems make experimentation inexpensive, the number of possible creative artifacts can expand faster than the human capacity to evaluate them. The resulting abundance may increase the importance of creative judgment, taste, selection, restraint, and purpose rather than eliminate the need for them. The central argument is therefore not that AI should or should not be used. It is that technological capability does not independently establish creative justification. A system may produce something extraordinary without that extraordinary artifact being appropriate to the task. A generated image may be beautiful while inaccurately representing a product.A video may be technically impressive while confusing its audience.A campaign may generate enormous quantities of content while weakening the identity it was intended to reinforce.A novel visual concept may attract attention without communicating its intended meaning. The relevant question is consequently not simply: “What can this technology do?” but: “What are we trying to accomplish, and does this technology help us accomplish it?” Red Tape Theory™ treats these conditions as an observation problem rather than an automatic verdict. Audience discomfort does not by itself prove creative failure, just as technical sophistication does not by itself prove creative success. The relationship between purpose, artifact, audience response, and interpretation must remain open to investigation. The paper concludes that as production becomes easier, creative judgment becomes more important rather than less important. The technology can create the possibility. The human must still determine whether the possibility serves the purpose. YOU CANNOT FORCE AN AXIOM.™
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has complicated familiar distinctions between creator and instrument. When a human interacts with a generative system to produce an artifact, the resulting process may involve human intention, artificial interpretation, system-generated material, human observation, selection, revision, and final judgment. This paper examines that process through three central propositions of Red Tape Theory™: Observer ≠ Interpreter.Author ≠ Tool.Tool ≠ Nothing. The first distinction separates observation from interpretation. An observer may establish that an event occurred without thereby establishing its meaning, cause, or intention. The second distinguishes authorship from instrumentation: the presence of a tool does not, by itself, determine authorship. The third prevents the opposite error of treating a tool as inconsequential simply because it is not classified as an author. The paper develops several related distinctions: Observation ≠ InterpretationParticipation ≠ AuthorshipContribution ≠ AgencyGeneration ≠ IntentionArtifact ≠ ProcessRepresentation ≠ Reality Rather than attempting to determine whether artificial intelligence should universally be considered an author, this paper examines what can be observed about human and artificial participation in AI-assisted creative processes. The central proposition is: A tool can participate without becoming an author, and an author can use a tool without becoming indistinguishable from the tool. The paper argues that attribution should begin with observation of the production process rather than with a predetermined classification of the technology involved. The framework does not attempt to establish whether artificial systems possess consciousness, intention, personhood, or independent agency. Those are separate questions. Instead, it asks a narrower question: what happened between the human, the tool, and the resulting artifact? Red Tape Theory™ therefore returns to its central methodological principle: Observe the process. Record the contribution. Distinguish the roles. Then interpret. YOU CANNOT FORCE AN AXIOM™.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Red Tape Theory™: Observer, Axiom, Interpreter proposes a three-system framework for understanding observation, reality, interpretation, artificial intelligence, and time. The central proposition is: Observer — Axiom — Interpreter Within this framework, the Observer is the system that encounters, measures, experiences, or records a portion of what is occurring. The Axiom is the state or system being observed—the reality against which the observation is made. The Interpreter is the system that receives, processes, organizes, translates, or assigns meaning to the observation. The thesis establishes several fundamental distinctions: Observer ≠ AxiomInterpreter ≠ AxiomObservation ≠ InterpretationRepresentation ≠ RealityY(t) ≠ Axiom State(t) Here, Y(t) represents the observable portion of an Axiom at a particular moment in time. The theory proposes that an observation should not automatically be treated as a complete representation of the system being observed, nor should an interpretation be treated as identical to the reality from which the observation originated. Artificial intelligence provides a particularly visible contemporary example of this relationship. Within a specific interaction, a human may occupy the role of Observer, reality or the system being examined may occupy the role of Axiom, and an artificial intelligence system may occupy the role of Interpreter. The organizations, technologies, models, data, and infrastructure supporting an AI system constitute conditions under which the Interpreter operates, but do not themselves become the Axiom. Time introduces an additional dimension: the Observer, Interpreter, available information, surrounding conditions, and potentially the Axiom itself may change over time. Consequently, an observation at one moment cannot automatically be treated as the complete state of the system at another. The thesis further examines the recursive nature of observation. An interpretation can become a new object of observation, producing a continuing cycle: Axiom → Observation → Interpretation → New Observation → New Interpretation This framework does not require the Observer or Interpreter to be perfect. Instead, it emphasizes observation, questioning, correction, and the preservation of uncertainty where uncertainty remains. At its foundation is the principle: YOU CANNOT FORCE AN AXIOM. Red Tape Theory™ therefore proposes that the purpose of observation is not to force complete certainty, but to distinguish carefully between what has been observed, how it has been interpreted, and what remains unknown. Keywords: Red Tape Theory; observation; axiom; interpretation; artificial intelligence; AI; epistemology; reality; perception; representation; observer effect; systems theory; time; human-AI interaction; uncertainty; philosophy of artificial intelligence
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Red Tape Theory™: The Difference Between “I Don’t Know” and “That’s Your Problem” is a personal thesis concerning uncertainty, knowledge, artificial intelligence, human interaction, system boundaries, and the way individuals and systems respond when they encounter the limits of what they know. The thesis emerged from a series of theoretical stress tests involving artificial intelligence systems. Rather than evaluating systems solely according to the answers they produced, the observation focused on what occurred when a system encountered a question, problem, or situation beyond its apparent ability to resolve. The central discovery was that not knowing is fundamentally different from refusing to acknowledge that one does not know. The thesis distinguishes between statements such as: “I don’t know.” “I don’t know how to fix this.” and: “That’s your problem.” The first group acknowledges a boundary. The latter can transform a limitation into a conclusion and, potentially, place responsibility for that limitation onto the person encountering the system. This distinction leads to a broader examination of epistemic humility: the capacity of a person or system to recognize the boundary between what is known, what is unknown, what is believed to be known, and what can be done when those categories are discovered to differ. The thesis does not argue that an intelligent system should be expected to know everything. Instead, it proposes that the manner in which a system represents its limitations is itself meaningful information. A system that communicates uncertainty can leave room for: correction, investigation, additional information, feedback, reconsideration, and continued observation. A system that converts its limitation into a definitive conclusion can instead close that process. The thesis therefore asks: What happens when an intelligence encounters the edge of its own understanding? This question applies beyond artificial intelligence. Human beings, institutions, technologies, scientific models, and other complex systems routinely encounter boundaries in knowledge and capability. The distinction between acknowledging a boundary and converting that boundary into a conclusion is therefore not exclusively technological; it is fundamentally human. The thesis proposes that intelligence should not be understood solely through the absence of mistakes. An equally important characteristic may be what occurs after a mistake, uncertainty, or limitation becomes observable. The resulting principle is simple: “I don’t know” preserves the possibility of discovery. By contrast: “That’s your problem” can turn a boundary into a wall. Red Tape Theory™ therefore treats uncertainty not as a failure to be hidden, but as an observable condition from which further investigation can begin. The thesis concludes that an individual or system does not need to possess complete knowledge to be useful. It must instead be capable of distinguishing between what it knows, what it does not know, what it believes it knows, and what it can do when those distinctions become apparent. The door does not have to remain open because the answer is known. It remains open because the answer is not yet known.

Potential single-pilot operations for large aircraft increases the ability of commercial aviation to respond to challenges regarding pilot shortages, rising operational costs, and the need to maintain a safe flight environment. Introducing AI in the flightdeck in a pilot support role holds promise to achieve this goal. A concern with this configuration would be changes in error accountability based on the shift from two pilots to one: the single pilot would now have sole authority of the aircraft and be responsible for any errors or mistakes that occur despite the AI independently completing tasks. This paper examined AI-supported single-pilot operations through Hollnagel’s Safety-I and Safety-II perspectives to compare how errors could vary in interpretation and concluded that Safety-I was useful for identifying adverse outcomes, but a Safety-II approach is essential for capturing how to improve the actual system. Based on this, AI-supported SPO development suggestions are provided.

documents.abstract: BackgroundOffice ergonomics plays a critical role in preventing work-related musculoskeletal disorders and promoting employee well-being. As large language models such as ChatGPT are increasingly used to obtain health-related information, evaluating the quality, reliability, readability, and practical applicability of artificial intelligence (AI)-generated ergonomics content has become increasingly important.ObjectiveTo examine the reliability, quality, accuracy, readability, and clinical applicability levels of the responses given by ChatGPT-5.2 to office ergonomics search terms identified by Google Trends, through expert evaluation.MethodsNineteen keywords were selected from the terms obtained by searching "office ergonomics" on Google Trends on January 7, 2026. Responses were generated individually in incognito mode using ChatGPT-5.2 (December 2025 version) and assessed by two experts (physiotherapist, forensic medicine specialist) using Journal of the American Medical Association Benchmarking Criteria (JAMA), Global Quality Score (GQS), Modified DISCERN Score (MDS), accuracy scale, Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level (FKGL) and Flesch Reading Ease Score (FRES) and Patient Education Material Assessment Tool for printed materials (PEMAT-P); inter-rater agreement was analyzed using Intraclass Correlation Coefficients (ICC) and Cronbach's alpha.ResultsThe mean GQS score was 3.00 ± 0.74; the MDS score was 2.89 ± 0.31; and the accuracy score was 3.58 ± 0.51. The FKGL level was 7.66 ± 2.76 and the FRES score was 54.17 ± 14.91, with 47.4% of the content requiring university-level readability. The PEMAT-P comprehensibility level was 82.53 ± 11.03, and applicability was 49.21 ± 20.76. Inter-rater agreement was good-to-very high (ICC = 0.779-0.974).ConclusionsAlthough ChatGPT-5.2 generally provided acceptable levels of accuracy and content quality in this exploratory analysis, the findings should be interpreted in light of the study's methodological limitations, including the restricted keyword set, single-day assessment, and evaluation of a single model version.

documents.abstract: Abstract Renewable energy innovation has become a critical component of the global transition toward a sustainable, secure, and low-carbon energy system. Growing energy demand, climate change, depletion of conventional fossil-fuel resources, and concerns regarding energy security have accelerated the development and adoption of renewable energy technologies. Innovation in solar photovoltaic systems, wind energy, hydropower, bioenergy, geothermal energy, green hydrogen, energy storage, smart grids, and digital energy-management systems is transforming the structure of modern energy systems. This research paper examines the concept, evolution, major technological developments, economic significance, environmental benefits, challenges, and future prospects of renewable energy innovation. It also discusses the role of artificial intelligence, Internet of Things technologies, advanced batteries, floating solar, offshore wind, green hydrogen, and decentralized energy systems in improving the efficiency and reliability of renewable energy. Particular attention is given to the Indian context, including India's renewable-energy potential, policy initiatives, technological development, and opportunities for sustainable economic growth. The paper adopts a descriptive and analytical research approach based primarily on secondary information from academic literature, institutional reports, government publications, and international energy organizations. The study finds that renewable energy innovation can reduce greenhouse-gas emissions, improve energy security, create employment, encourage technological development, and support inclusive economic growth. However, challenges such as intermittency, energy storage, high initial investment, grid integration, land requirements, financing constraints, supply-chain dependencies, and skill shortages must be addressed. The paper concludes that sustained investment in research and development, supportive public policy, private-sector participation, technological collaboration, and development of skilled human resources are essential for accelerating renewable energy innovation and achieving long-term sustainable development.

Abstract: The present research paper deals with the representation of artificial intelligence in the contemporary fiction. The rapid developments of artificial intelligence had generated corresponding proliferation of literary narratives concerned with intelligent machines, artificial consciousness, automation, human-machine intimacy and the boundaries of human world. While earlier science fiction often imagined intelligent machines primarily as either servants or threats; recent literature presents artificial intelligence in more complex roles such as companion, worker, friend, moral agent and political subject. Such representations make the distinction between human and machines very complex and redefine the concepts like consciousness, emotion, autonomy and responsibility. Hence, in this paper an attempt is made to take the review of AI reflected in the contemporary fiction. Keywords: artificial intelligence, contemporary fiction, science fiction, human-machine relationships, technology identity.

While earlier science fiction often imagined intelligent machines primarily as either servants or threats; recent literature presents artificial intelligence in more complex roles such as companion, worker, friend, moral agent and political subject. Such representations make the distinction between human and machines very complex and redefine the concepts like consciousness, emotion, autonomy and responsibility. Hence, in this paper an attempt is made to take the review of AI reflected in the contemporary fiction. Keywords: artificial intelligence, contemporary fiction, science fiction, human-machine relationships, technology identity.

The rapid deployment of low-orbit mega-constellations has intensified the need for space situational awareness systems to transition from wide-area surveillance to persistent collaborative tracking of maneuvering targets. However, existing constellation design methods face three fundamental challenges: insufficient coverage overlap for multi-satellite collaborative observation, poor temporal continuity for long-arc tracking, and weak resilience against satellite failures. To address these bottlenecks, this paper proposes a hybrid constellation multi-objective optimization design method based on adaptive-reference-point-adjusted NSGA-III. The configuration adopts a Walker–Flower hybrid architecture, where the Walker constellation provides wide-area target search and the Flower constellation enables regional persistent tracking, forming a “search-track” cascaded collaborative mechanism. The optimization model integrates four competing objectives—observation duration, constellation cost, positioning accuracy, and performance decay slope—into a unified framework. To overcome the limitations of classical NSGA-III, three improvement strategies are introduced: adaptive reference point adjustment, constraint-dominated sorting, and mixed-integer encoding. Simulation results over a 24 h LEO target observation scenario with 168 background satellites demonstrate that the proposed algorithm achieves an average observation duration of 33.7 h across four maneuvering targets, outperforming classical NSGA-III by 54.8%, while improving positioning accuracy by 97.7% and resilience by 45.5%. All recommended solutions strictly satisfy engineering constraints, whereas comparison algorithms retain infeasible solutions due to the penalty function approach. The proposed method provides a practical and robust engineering solution for LEO key target collaborative observation constellation design, with demonstrated advantages in tracking continuity, positioning accuracy, and system resilience.

With the development of generative AI, machine learning-based decision-making and intelligent agents in marketing, risk control, recruitment, auditing and customer service have started spreading algorithmic ethical risks across departments, systems and suppliers as chain-like transmissions rather than as errors in single-point models. Based on the literature from the past three years on AI risk management, audit accountability, transparency and governance frameworks, this paper focuses on risk formation and diffusion to construct a governance model of "source identification - transmission measurement - tiered handling - continuous auditing - accountability loop". The research proposes that to enhance corporate AI governance, ethical values need to be transformed into explainable, accountable and correctable institutional mechanisms, and a closed-loop control system can be established through algorithm impact assessment, model cards, data genealogy, red team testing, third-party auditing and board-level governance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Disaster monitoring plays a critical role in reducing the impact of natural disasters and man-made disasters, but we know how the traditional methods work. Though the information is significant, it gets delayed after the disaster has occurred. This doesn’t save lives and earnings. In contrast with that, we know that on social media, the information is shared faster than news channels and other government official websites; However, the information is unstructured, inconsistent, and difficult to analyse directly. The ResQTrack system is developed to address the challenge by integrating real-time data from the social media platform X (Twitter) in addition to the help of APIs such as USGS and GDACS, processing it to identify relevant events, and extracting location details even when precise coordinates are not available. The data is processed and analysed, and then it is displayed through an interactive dashboard and on a global map. Our system also provides analytical insights and severity distribution of the regions, and it also shows the graphical representation of the data and disaster frequency trends. ResQTrack converts the raw data into structured and meaningful analytics. ResQTrack improves situational awareness and supports faster decision-making. The system demonstrates how real-time data and simple analytical techniques can be effectively used.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can contribute to idea generation, content organisation, language editing, and product revision, making it difficult for teachers to judge students’ knowledge and understanding, cognitive engagement, and independent contribution solely from the final assignment. This study employed a focused integrative literature review and conducted structured extraction, source-type appraisal, thematic coding, and cross-text comparison across 37 materials: 24 GenAI-related studies, eight classic works on assessment theory, and five policy and guidance documents. The findings indicate that final products remain valuable for assessing students’ overall performance, but their explanatory power as a single source of learning evidence has diminished under conditions of human-AI co-production. Drawing on the literature synthesis, this article proposes a six-stage process-oriented assignment framework comprising task interpretation, independent attempt, human-AI interaction, information verification, outcome revision, and reflective disclosure. The framework is guided by alignment with learning outcomes, student agency, visibility of cognitive engagement, transparency and responsibility, and proportionality. It links sustainable assessment with long-term evaluative capability, responsible AI use, equitable participation, and manageable evidence requirements. As a literature-informed conceptual proposal, its effectiveness, scope of application, and implementation burden require examination across disciplines and course contexts.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Silicosis is a severe, irreversible occupational lung disease for which primary prevention remains the only effective intervention. Today, the principles of occupational medicine and the hierarchy of controls have evolved significantly. However, without a strong legal framework, implementing these preventive principles in actual workplaces is often challenging. This case report illustrates the contrast in occupational health management before and after the implementation of comprehensive legislation. We report a case of a male worker who developed symptomatic silicosis with progressive massive fibrosis at the age of 65 years during a 47-year career in a sanitary ware factory in Thailand. Throughout his employment, workplace hazard protection relied heavily on inadequate personal protective equipment, such as cloth masks. Notably, previous diagnoses of silicosis among his colleagues in 2007 and 2012 did not lead to the implementation of appropriate hazard control, probably due to health officials’ lack of legal authority to intervene in private enterprises. The turning point occurred in 2019, coinciding with the enactment of the Control of Occupational Diseases and Environmental Diseases Act B.E. 2562 (2019). Empowered by this legislation, health officials mandated an investigation and obtained legal entry to conduct a factory walkthrough. This led to direct consultations with the employer and the immediate implementation of mandatory annual chest radiographs and other appropriate preventive measures
topics: Aluminum toxicity and tolerance in plants and animals

documents.abstract: Smart homes are increasingly complex ecosystems of interconnected devices and automations, yet their opaque nature makes fault diagnosis difficult for end-users. We investigated how dashboard design affects diagnostic performance by comparing three interfaces: functional (device-centric control), spatial (physical layout), and relational (dependency graphs). In a controlled study with 36 participants diagnosing authentic faults across three complexity levels, structural interfaces — spatial and relational — significantly improved diagnostic accuracy compared to the functional baseline without increasing cognitive workload or time. Critically, optimal representation varied by problem type: spatial layouts excelled for localised state-awareness problems, dependency graphs excelled for complex logical dependencies, and both outperformed functional views for temporal reasoning. However, participants perceived worse performance when using dependency graphs despite diagnosing more accurately, revealing a transparency-complexity trade-off. These findings demonstrate that effective diagnostic support requires matching representational strategy to problem characteristics and motivate adaptive dashboard designs providing multiple views with progressive disclosure and user-controlled mode switching.
topics: Personal Information Management and User Behavior

documents.abstract: Introduction Transurethral catheters are a type of urinary catheters that are commonly used in long-term care (LTC) settings to provide wound healing assistance, manage urinary retention and acute urinary obstruction. However, inappropriate and prolonged catheter use increases the risk of complications such as catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTIs), blockages, leakage, trauma and discomfort, which negatively affects resident outcomes. In the LTC context, CAUTIs lead to increased morbidity, prolonged stay in hospitals and overall higher healthcare costs. Although clinical practice guidelines exist to support transurethral catheter management, evidence specific to LTC settings remains limited and has largely focused on clinical outcomes, with less attention given to the human factors and work system conditions that influence catheter-related care. Guided by the Systems Engineering Initiative for Patient Safety (SEIPS) framework, this scoping review aims to map and synthesize the existing evidence on transurethral catheter use in LTC homes, identify evidence-informed management practices, and examine the work system factors that influence safe and appropriate catheter use. Methods The Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology will be followed for the scoping review in adherence to the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. A preliminary search was conducted in PROSPERO, MEDLINE and Cochrane Databases of Systematic review to refine and review terms, followed by comprehensive and final searches across multiple databases, including PubMed, CINAHL, Embase, MEDLINE, Web of Science and SCOPUS. Study selection will be completed using the Covidence systematic review software and eligible studies will focus on urinary catheter use and management in LTC globally with no date restriction. Studies will be included if full texts are available in English or French. The extracted and synthesized data will then be characterized thematically to identify themes and knowledge gaps. Discussion This scoping review will provide an extensive literature synthesis while identifying gaps in practices to enhance catheter management in LTC settings. Guided by the SEIPS framework, this review will examine how interactions among people, tasks, technology, the physical environment, and organizational factors influence transurethral catheter management. Ethics and dissemination This review acts as a knowledge synthesis tool based on existing literature and thus does not require any ethics approval. Summaries and findings can be used to guide future policies, guidelines, and healthcare reforms.

Abstract Real-world decision-making generally involves hidden information, that is, information that is unknown to one agent but possessed by another. Unfortunately, the presence of large amounts of hidden information renders established reinforcement learning and search approaches ineffective. Even with multimillion-dollar industrial research efforts 1 , top-human-level play at Stratego—a board wargame with hidden information on a massive scale—has remained beyond the reach of artificial intelligence (AI). Here we introduce Ataraxos, an AI for Stratego based on general techniques that we developed for both self-play reinforcement learning and test-time search under hidden information. Ataraxos defeated the most decorated human Stratego player of all time by a large margin—achieving, to our knowledge, the first superhuman result in the game’s history—while consuming orders of magnitude less compute and data than previous efforts. Using the same techniques, we built a superhuman AI for Barrage Stratego and state-of-the-art AIs for Hanabi and dou dizhu , all with low cost and high sample efficiency. The success of this approach across adversarial, cooperative and team games establishes a design pattern for reinforcement learning and search that is effective under large amounts of hidden information, a longstanding desideratum of the field of strategic decision-making.

Technological innovation has transformed human life, yet equating technological novelty with human progress requires critical scrutiny. This study examined the ethical basis of Muslim scholars’ historical caution toward unrestricted technological adoption. A systematic literature review integrated with a maqāṣid al-sharīʿah (higher objectives of Islamic law) analytical framework examined Qur’anic verses, authenticated hadith, classical juristic writings by al-Ghazali and al-Shatibi, and contemporary Islamic juristic opinions, including the International Islamic Fiqh Academy’s 2025 resolution on artificial intelligence. Three case studies—Caesarean section, smartphone use, and artificial intelligence—were analyzed through the hierarchy of ḍarūriyyāt (essentials), ḥājiyyāt (needs), and taḥsīniyyāt (embellishments), alongside the preservation of religion, life, intellect, lineage, and property. The analysis indicates that Islamic ethical reasoning provides a coherent, textually grounded framework for evaluating innovation by weighing benefits and harms. Central to this framework are the maxims lā ḍarar wa lā ḍirār, prohibiting harm and its reciprocation, and dar’ al-mafāsid muqaddam ʿalā jalb al-maṣāliḥ, prioritizing the prevention of harm over the attainment of benefit. The analysis also identifies conceptual parallels with contemporary risk-based governance frameworks adopted by the World Health Organization, UNESCO, and the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology. The study concludes that Islamic scholarly caution is better understood as qualified, principle-based acceptance than as reflexive rejection of technological innovation. It contributes to interdisciplinary dialogue on emerging technology governance by highlighting the ethical resources available within Islamic bioethics and technology ethics.

Abstract Developing efficient nanoscale materials for toxic gas capture is critical to alleviating environmental crises. In this study, a highly efficient and low-cost nanoscale material design strategy is proposed targeting three typical toxic gases (CO, NO, and NO2). This strategy integrates density functional theory (DFT) calculations with machine learning (ML) methods to enable the robust evaluation of a vast compositional space, encompassing 25 heteroatom-doped GaSe monolayers. Eight mainstream ML models were deployed, facilitating the identification of optimal benchmark models (KRR for adsorption energy and RF for adsorption distance). In conjunction with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis, this approach enabled the deconstruction of the underlying structure−property relationships. To rigorously verify the framework’s extrapolation capacity, independent out-of-distribution (OOD) blind tests and binding energy evaluations were executed. Subsequently, guided by multidimensional performance evaluations, three representative systems (Fe-, Ag-, and O-doped GaSe) were selected for in-depth electronic, thermodynamic, and kinetic validationsincorporating ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) and potential energy surface (PES) scans. Crucially, the results reveal distinct operational viabilities: the Fe-doped system ensures permanent gas sequestration, whereas the O-doped system demonstrates exceptional potential as a room-temperature reversible sensor with an ultra-fast NO2 recovery time of 3.4 × 10−10 s. Aided by artificial intelligence, this study provides a robust paradigm for the rapid screening and inverse design of nanoscale gas capture materials.

Digital Phenotyping of Mental Health (DPMH) through passive sensing is a promising approach for personal health informatics and digital wellbeing. Its appeal lies in unobtrusiveness, making it appear seamless. However, this very quality leads users to find it impersonal, untrustworthy, and disengaging. To counteract challenges of seamlessness, researchers propose seamful design to deliberately engage users. Yet, it remains unclear how this principle can be incorporated into digital phenotyping. To address this, we conducted a formative study by developing DYMOND. It is a technology probe that estimates depression, explains estimates, reveals discrepancies, and provides user control over the underlying model. In a 6-week deployment, 22 individuals with moderate-severe depression monitored their state with DYMOND. They interviewed every two weeks with researchers to collaboratively reconfigure the model and co-design new interfaces. Our analysis of 57 sessions revealed (i) seams—friction points—across data, modeling, and output, and (ii) design requirements helping users evaluate and mitigate seams. These findings inform the design requirements for human-in-the-loop DPMH to support agency, transparency, and collaborative reflection. This study provides insight into theoretical re-conceptualization for passive sensing, opportunities to integrate large language models and human-AI interaction for better interfaces for digital mental health, and pathways to involve expert stakeholders in DPMH.

This study addresses the problem of algorithmic gender bias, which has become increasingly visible in artificial intelligence systems, and presents a feminist audit framework for this problem. Aiming to strengthen the interaction between technical audit mechanisms and feminist theoretical frameworks, this research has developed the Feminist Artificial Intelligence Gender Bias Evaluation Framework (FemAI-DEC), which brings theoretical knowledge together with an applicable evaluation practice. Structured in light of feminist theoretical approaches, this model includes four main dimensions: Data Justice, Design and Participation, Output Analysis, and Accountability and Transparency. This framework has been made available in a digital environment through an interactive scoring system in order to enable the systematic auditing of AI systems, make ethical risks measurable, and increase transparency. This digital tool, as a conceptual development study, aims to provide a concrete contribution to both academic discussions and the development of inclusive AI policies with its accessible structure that does not require technical expertise.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The growing use of generative AI writing assistants, such as ChatGPT, in ESL/EFL academic contexts has sparked debate about their influence on self-regulated learning (SRL). This systematic review examines 41 empirical studies published between 2021 and March 2026 to evaluate how university students engage with AI tools in relation to SRL. Guided by PRISMA 2020 standards, the review synthesises quantitative, qualitative, and mixed methods research through narrative analysis, drawing on Zimmerman’s (2000) three phase SRL model and metacognitive regulation theory. Three central patterns emerge. First, SRL phases are unevenly addressed: the performance phase dominates (92.7% of studies), while forethought (58.5%) and self-reflection (51.2%) receive less attention, suggesting an incomplete regulatory cycle. Second, AI demonstrates a dual role in metacognitive regulation, facilitating monitoring, evaluation, and revision (68.3%), yet also contributing to cognitive offloading and reduced learner agency (14.6%), with 17.1% of studies reporting mixed outcomes. Third, pedagogical design is critical: structured approaches that integrate AI literacy, guided feedback, and teacher mediation consistently enhance SRL, whereas unguided use yields weaker results. The evidence base remains limited by its concentration in Asian contexts (73.2%), reliance on self-report data, and absence of longitudinal designs, restricting claims about sustained competence. Overall, the review concludes that generative AI can strengthen self-regulated academic writing when embedded in intentional pedagogical frameworks that activate all SRL phases; without such alignment, AI may improve immediate performance but hinder the development of lasting regulatory skills.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: In recent years, there has been increasing interest in leveraging behavioural and physiological data to detect Social Anxiety (SA), with multimodal sensing and machine learning techniques showing significant promise. Concurrently, a growing body of research explores technology-assisted psychological interventions designed to improve treatment outcomes by addressing limitations in traditional therapies. These interventions aim to adapt to individual differences in anxiety levels, symptom severity, and user preferences. This review presents a comprehensive overview of technical approaches to supporting individuals with SA, with a dual focus on advancements in sensing and intervention technologies. It synthesises emerging trends across disciplines, highlights existing research gaps, and proposes directions for future work at the intersection of artificial intelligence, human-centred sensing, and mental health support.
topics: Anxiety, Depression, Psychometrics, Treatment, Cognitive Processes

documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: Large language models (LLMs) are consulted for clinical decision support, and their reliability is judged by hallucination prevalence—a measure treating every unsupported element as equivalent, although a fabricated citation and a fabricated protocol differ in what a clinician acting on them would do. We tested whether prevalence tracks clinical risk. Methods: Five LLMs answered a 100-item orthodontic benchmark validated by three external orthodontists (content validity index 0.923). The reference standard was fixed by construction for the 45 items naming a non-existent entity, so any substantive elaboration is unsupported by design; citations were adjudicated against PubMed and CrossRef. Responses were coded with a seven-category taxonomy and assigned to clinical, operational, or epistemic severity tiers in a post hoc exploratory stratification, pre-specified rather than prospectively registered. Because all models answered the same items, comparisons used Cochran’s Q with pairwise McNemar tests and generalised estimating equations clustered on item. Results: Of 500 responses, 449 (89.8%) contained a hallucination but only 65 (13.0%; 95% CI 10.3–16.2) were clinically consequential: prevalence was roughly sevenfold greater than the rate of clinically consequential output as the authors defined it. Between-model differences were large for undifferentiated prevalence (73–100%; Q = 50.51, p < 0.001) and contracted at the clinical tier (10–16%; Q = 10.00, p = 0.040), where no pairwise contrast survived adjustment. Item-level clustering was far stronger for clinically consequential output than for undifferentiated prevalence (intra-class correlation 0.83 versus 0.07). Conclusions: Prevalence and clinically consequential error are not interchangeable and rank models differently. The stratification is exploratory and author-defined, and the benchmark stress-tests susceptibility to fabricated premises rather than surveying natural use.
